title: AKS: Node Pools, Autoscaling & App Gateway Ingress
summary: Design AKS node pools, drive the cluster autoscaler, triage Pending pods and stalled node provisioning with the full panel checklist, and expose workloads through Application Gateway ingress — answering every AKS panel question cold.
objectives: Justify multiple node pools over one giant pool across SKU, scaling, cost, and blast-radius dimensions
Configure the cluster autoscaler and manual scaling with az aks nodepool scale/update, including min/max semantics
Diagnose Pending pods from kubectl describe events and distinguish scheduler causes from cloud-side provisioning failures
Apply taints, tolerations, and labels correctly to control pod placement
Expose AKS workloads through Application Gateway with AGIC, contrasting L7 and L4 exposure

notes.title: Why Multiple Node Pools Beat One Giant Pool
notes.body: An AKS node pool is a group of nodes that share the same VM size, OS, and scaling configuration. Every cluster starts with at least one system node pool (which runs kube-system pods like CoreDNS and metrics-server) plus one or more user node pools for your workloads. The panel question is direct: what is the benefit of multiple pools versus one giant pool? First, blast radius and upgrade safety: you can cordon, drain, and upgrade one pool at a time instead of rolling the entire fleet at once. Second, heterogeneous hardware: GPU workloads, memory-heavy caches, and cheap spot VMs cannot share one VM SKU, so each gets its own pool. Third, scaling independence: the cluster autoscaler scales each pool against its own min/max, so a batch queue bursting at night never steals capacity planning from the latency-sensitive API pool. Fourth, cost: you can run steady workloads on reserved/priced VMs in one pool and elastic overflow on spot in another. Worked example: design pools for a payments API with steady traffic plus a nightly reconciliation batch. Solution: (1) system pool: 3 x Standard_D4s_v5, autoscaler disabled, min=max=3 for control-plane-adjacent stability; (2) user pool 'apipool': Standard_D8s_v5, min 4 max 20 with autoscaler, taint-free so API pods schedule freely; (3) user pool 'batchpool': spot VMs, min 0 max 30, tainted spot=true:NoSchedule so only batch jobs with the matching toleration land there. One giant pool forces a single VM size, a single upgrade blast radius, and a single scaling policy — three compromises you never need to accept.

notes.title: How the Cluster Autoscaler Thinks
notes.body: The cluster autoscaler watches for pods that cannot be scheduled and adds nodes; it watches for underutilized nodes and removes them. Scale-up triggers when a pod stays Pending because no existing node has room — the autoscaler simulates scheduling, picks the pool that fits, and calls the Azure API to grow that pool, bounded by --max-count. Scale-down is conservative: a node becomes eligible only after all its pods can move elsewhere and it has been underutilized (default under 50% requested resources) for about 10 minutes, and it never removes nodes running kube-system pods it cannot evict. Two limits shape every design. First, max pods per node: with Azure CNI each pod consumes a VNet IP, so a Standard_D4s_v5 node might cap at 30 pods; with Azure CNI Overlay, pods use overlay IPs and the cap rises toward 250. Second, the pool's min/max counts are hard ceilings the autoscaler will not cross. Worked example: your API needs 120 pod replicas, each requesting 0.5 CPU, on D8s_v5 nodes (8 vCPUs, 30-pod cap with Azure CNI). CPU math: 120 x 0.5 = 60 vCPUs / 8 per node = 7.5, so 8 nodes by CPU. Pod-count math: 120 / 30 = 4 nodes. The binding constraint is CPU: 8 nodes. Solution: set the pool to min 4 (steady state) and max 12 (headroom for the burst plus rolling-update surge), and let the autoscaler float between them; a max of 8 would deadlock a rolling update that temporarily needs extra nodes.

notes.title: Manual Scaling: az aks nodepool scale and update
notes.body: The panel asks how to manually increase the maximum nodes per pool, and the answer is the Azure CLI, not the portal. To change the live node count immediately: az aks nodepool scale --resource-group myRG --cluster-name myAKS --name apipool --node-count 8. To change the autoscaler's bounds: az aks nodepool update --resource-group myRG --cluster-name myAKS --name apipool --enable-cluster-autoscaler --min-count 4 --max-count 20. To disable the autoscaler and pin a count: az aks nodepool update --resource-group myRG --cluster-name myAKS --name apipool --disable-cluster-autoscaler followed by a scale command. Know the precedence: a manual scale sets node-count inside the min/max window; if the autoscaler is enabled it may scale back down within minutes, so pinning the count without disabling the autoscaler is a classic exam trap. Worked example: on-call at 2 AM, pods are Pending with 'Insufficient cpu', and the pool shows max-count 6 with 6 nodes running. The autoscaler cannot help — it is already at its ceiling. Solution: run az aks nodepool update with --max-count 12 (keep --min-count as-is), then watch kubectl get nodes; within a few minutes new nodes join and Pending pods schedule. If instead the pool had 3 nodes against a max of 12 and pods were still Pending, raising the ceiling would do nothing — the problem is elsewhere (quotas, taints, or subnet IPs), which is exactly the triage in the next note.

notes.title: Pod Stuck in Pending: The Triage Runbook
notes.body: A pod in Pending means the scheduler could not place it. Start with kubectl describe pod <name> and read the Events section — the FailedScheduling message names the cause: 'Insufficient cpu', 'Insufficient memory', or 'didn't match pod affinity'. If it says insufficient resources, the panel's follow-up is 'out of nodes — how do you fix it?': raise the pool's max count (previous note) and confirm the autoscaler has room. When new nodes still do not appear, walk the full triage checklist the panel expects: (1) cluster autoscaler logs — is it even attempting scale-up? (2) Azure subscription quotas — vCPU quota per region and per VM family; (3) region capacity — the SKU may be unavailable in that zone; (4) taints and tolerations — nodes exist but pods cannot tolerate their taints; (5) labels and node selectors — a nodeSelector pointing at a label no node carries; (6) service principal / managed identity permissions — the cluster identity cannot create VMs; (7) Azure Activity log — failed VM creation operations with error codes; (8) Azure Monitor / Resource Health — platform issues; (9) subnet IP space — with Azure CNI, no free IPs means no new nodes; (10) VM SKU restrictions — policy or subscription blocks the SKU; (11) Azure Policy assignments denying the deployment; (12) max pods per node already saturated. Worked example: describe shows '0/5 nodes are available: 5 Insufficient cpu', the pool is at max-count 6/6, and the Activity log shows a failed deployment with error 'OperationNotAllowed - quota exceeded'. Solution: quota is the blocker — request a vCPU quota increase for that VM family in that region, then raise max-count. Scaling commands cannot fix a quota denial.

notes.title: Taints, Tolerations, and Labels: The Scheduling Vocabulary
notes.body: Labels, taints, and tolerations are three different scheduling controls and the panel asks you to distinguish them. Labels are key/value metadata on nodes and pods used for selection: kubectl label nodes node1 workload=api, then a pod's nodeSelector: {workload: api} restricts it to matching nodes. Labels attract; they never repel. Taints repel: kubectl taint nodes node1 sku=gpu:NoSchedule marks the node so only pods that tolerate the taint may schedule there. The three effects are NoSchedule (new pods blocked), PreferNoSchedule (soft preference), and NoExecute (existing pods evicted too — used for node problems like disk pressure). Tolerations are the pod-side opt-in, declared in the pod spec: tolerations: [{key: sku, operator: Equal, value: gpu, effect: NoSchedule}]. A common production pattern is tainting the system pool so user workloads can never land on it: kubectl taint nodes -l kubernetes.azure.com/mode=system CriticalAddonsOnly=true:NoSchedule. Worked example: GPU nodes sit idle while GPU pods stay Pending with 'didn't match toleration'. Solution: the nodes were tainted sku=gpu:NoSchedule but the deployment lacks the toleration — add the toleration block above to the pod template, or remove the taint if GPU isolation is no longer needed. Remember the asymmetry the panel probes: a pod without a toleration can never schedule on a tainted node, but a pod with a toleration may still schedule on untainted nodes — tolerations permit, they do not require.

notes.title: Application Gateway Ingress: L7 Traffic into AKS
notes.body: The panel asks about exposing Kubernetes endpoints through Application Gateway and how it differs from a Load Balancer. An Azure Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP): it forwards packets to backend IPs without understanding HTTP. Application Gateway operates at Layer 7: it terminates TLS, reads HTTP hostnames and paths, and routes to different backend pools — exactly what an Ingress controller needs. The Azure Application Gateway Ingress Controller (AGIC) runs as a pod in your cluster, watches Ingress resources, and programs the Application Gateway accordingly, so developers declare routing in YAML and AGIC translates it to gateway config. Traffic flow for a browser request: DNS resolves your hostname to the Application Gateway's public IP, the gateway terminates TLS and matches the host/path rule, then forwards to the AKS nodes' backend pool, where kube-proxy routes to the pod. Worked example: expose shop.example.com/api to the api service and shop.example.com/ to the web service. Solution — an Ingress with the annotation kubernetes.io/ingress.class: azure/application-gateway and rules: [{host: shop.example.com, http: {paths: [{path: /api/*, backend: {service: {name: api, port: {number: 80}}}}, {path: /*, backend: {service: {name: web, port: {number: 80}}}]}}]. Add the WAF tier (WAF_v2) on the gateway for OWASP rule protection at the edge. Know the contrast cold: need raw TCP passthrough or ultra-low latency? Load Balancer (L4). Need host/path routing, TLS termination, or WAF? Application Gateway (L7).

quiz.q: A payments API (steady) and a nightly batch job (bursty, fault-tolerant) share one giant AKS node pool. What is the strongest reason to split them into two pools?
choices: Two pools double the Kubernetes version
Independent autoscaler min/max and VM SKUs let the batch pool use spot VMs at min 0 while the API pool stays stable
Node pools are required for kubectl to work
A single pool cannot exceed 3 nodes
quiz.explain: Separate pools give each workload its own VM SKU, scaling bounds, and upgrade blast radius — the batch pool can run cheap spot VMs scaled to zero while the API pool holds steady capacity.

quiz.q: Pods are Pending with 'Insufficient cpu'. The pool shows 6/6 nodes and max-count is 6. What is the correct first fix?
choices: Raise the pool's max-count with az aks nodepool update
quiz.explain: The autoscaler is already at its ceiling, so it cannot add nodes. Raising --max-count gives it room; deleting pods or raising limits does not create capacity.

quiz.q: After raising max-count, still no new nodes appear. The Azure Activity log shows 'OperationNotAllowed' quota errors. What is the blocker?
choices: Subscription vCPU quota for that VM family/region is exhausted
quiz.explain: OperationNotAllowed quota errors mean Azure refused the VM creation — no CLI scaling command can fix this; you must request a quota increase, then scale.

quiz.q: Which kubectl command applies a repelling mark so that only specially-marked pods schedule on GPU nodes?
quiz.explain: kubectl taint with effect NoSchedule repels pods; only pods declaring a matching toleration may schedule there. Labels attract, cordon blocks all scheduling.

quiz.q: A pod spec has nodeSelector {workload: api} but stays Pending although nodes exist. What should you check first?
choices: Whether any node actually carries the label workload=api
quiz.explain: nodeSelector only matches nodes carrying that exact label; a typo'd or missing label is the classic cause. Verify with kubectl get nodes -l workload=api.

quiz.q: Why choose Application Gateway over Azure Load Balancer for exposing a web app on AKS?
choices: Layer 7 routing: host/path rules, TLS termination, and WAF at the edge
It works without any Ingress resource
quiz.explain: App Gateway understands HTTP — host/path routing, TLS termination, WAF — while a Load Balancer only forwards TCP/UDP (L4). AGIC still needs Ingress resources to program it.

quiz.q: What does AGIC do in an AKS cluster?
choices: It watches Ingress resources and configures the Azure Application Gateway
It issues TLS certificates from Azure Key Vault
quiz.explain: The Application Gateway Ingress Controller runs in-cluster, watches Ingress objects, and translates them into Application Gateway backend pools, listeners, and routing rules.

quiz.q: The autoscaler removed a node 12 minutes after it became idle, killing a long-running batch pod. Which behavior explains this?
choices: Scale-down of underutilized nodes after the ~10-minute delay; batch pods need protection via PodDisruptionBudgets or dedicated tainted pools
The node ran out of disk
quiz.explain: Scale-down evicts moveable pods after roughly 10 minutes of underutilization. Long-running or stateful work belongs on protected/dedicated pools, not mixed with elastic capacity.

quiz.q: With Azure CNI, new nodes fail to join and the subnet shows no free IPs. What is happening?
choices: Each pod consumes a VNet IP, so IP exhaustion blocks node provisioning — expand the subnet or switch to Overlay
The nodes need bigger OS disks
quiz.explain: Azure CNI assigns real VNet IPs to pods, so a full subnet stops both pod scheduling and node joins. Overlay mode avoids this by using overlay IPs.

drills.title: Timed drill: node pool and autoscaler decisions

items.prompt: 90 seconds: state the benefit of multiple node pools vs one giant pool.
items.answer: Independent VM SKUs, autoscaler min/max per pool, smaller upgrade blast radius, cost mixing (spot vs on-demand), workload isolation.
items.explain: Hit all five: SKUs, scaling bounds, blast radius, cost, isolation. The panel wants the contrast, not just a definition.

items.prompt: Command: set pool 'apipool' to exactly 8 nodes right now.
items.answer: az aks nodepool scale --resource-group myRG --cluster-name myAKS --name apipool --node-count 8
items.explain: scale sets the live count. If the autoscaler is enabled it may drift back — disable it first for a pinned count.

items.prompt: Command: enable the autoscaler on 'apipool' with min 3, max 15.
items.answer: az aks nodepool update --resource-group myRG --cluster-name myAKS --name apipool --enable-cluster-autoscaler --min-count 3 --max-count 15
items.explain: update changes configuration; scale changes the live count. Mixing them up is the classic panel trap.

items.prompt: Pods Pending 'Insufficient memory', pool at 5/5 nodes, max-count 5. Fix?
items.answer: Raise the ceiling: az aks nodepool update ... --max-count <higher> (keep min). The autoscaler is capped.
items.explain: The autoscaler cannot exceed max-count. Raising it is the fix — but verify quota first if Activity log shows denials.

items.prompt: Max-count raised, still no nodes; Activity log shows quota 'OperationNotAllowed'. Next step?
items.answer: Request a vCPU quota increase for that VM family in that region, then confirm nodes join.
items.explain: Quota denials come from Azure policy on the subscription, not from Kubernetes — only a quota increase unblocks it.

items.prompt: Why taint the system node pool?
items.answer: So user workloads can never schedule on nodes running CoreDNS/metrics-server — e.g. taint CriticalAddonsOnly=true:NoSchedule.
items.explain: Protects cluster-critical pods from noisy neighbors and from scale-down eviction pressure.

items.prompt: Toleration vs nodeSelector: which one permits scheduling on a tainted node?
items.answer: Toleration. nodeSelector only attracts to labels; it cannot overcome a taint.
items.explain: Tolerations permit, never require; labels attract, never repel. Say the asymmetry explicitly.

drills.title: Timed drill: Pending-pod triage from events

items.prompt: Event: '0/4 nodes are available: 4 Insufficient cpu'. Pool 4/4, max 4. Diagnosis and fix?
items.answer: Scheduler found no CPU headroom and the pool is at its autoscaler ceiling. Fix: az aks nodepool update --max-count higher.
items.explain: Read the two facts together: insufficient CPU + at ceiling = raise the ceiling. Either fact alone changes the answer.

items.prompt: Event: 'didn't match pod affinity/anti-affinity'. What do you check?
items.answer: The pod's affinity rules vs actual node labels — kubectl get nodes --show-labels; fix the rule or label the nodes.
items.explain: Affinity mismatch is a label problem, not a capacity problem. Scaling never fixes it.

items.prompt: Nodes exist with free CPU but the pod has nodeSelector {gpu: 'true'} and stays Pending. Cause?
items.answer: No node carries label gpu=true. Add the label or correct the selector.
items.explain: nodeSelector is exact-match. Verify with kubectl get nodes -l gpu=true — empty result confirms it.

items.prompt: GPU nodes are Ready but GPU pods report 'toleration not matched'. Fix?
items.answer: Add the matching toleration to the pod template, or remove the NoSchedule taint from the nodes.
items.explain: Taint without toleration = Pending forever. The toleration key/value/effect must match the taint exactly.

items.prompt: New nodes fail: subnet has 0 free IPs, Azure CNI in use. Two remedies?
items.answer: Expand the subnet address space, or migrate the pool to Azure CNI Overlay so pods stop consuming VNet IPs.
items.explain: Azure CNI burns one VNet IP per pod — IP exhaustion blocks node joins entirely.

items.prompt: Name three non-Kubernetes places to check when nodes will not provision.
items.answer: Azure Activity log (failed operations), subscription vCPU quotas, Azure Policy assignments (deny rules).
items.explain: The panel's 'new nodes still not deploying' checklist lives half outside Kubernetes — say these three first, then region capacity, SKU restrictions, identity permissions.

items.prompt: Pod was Running, then suddenly restarts with no code change. Which probe do you suspect and what command confirms the reason?
items.answer: Suspect the liveness probe (it restarts containers). Confirm with kubectl describe pod — check Last State: Terminated, Reason, and Exit Code.
items.explain: Liveness failures trigger restarts; readiness only removes from service. describe shows lastState.terminated.reason (e.g. OOMKilled, Error) and exit code.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: multi-pool AKS with autoscaling and App Gateway ingress
handsOnLab.brief: You will provision an AKS cluster with separate system and user node pools, enable the cluster autoscaler, deploy the Application Gateway Ingress Controller, expose a sample app through host/path routing, and practice the Pending-pod triage commands. Estimated cloud cost is a few dollars if you delete the resource group the same day.
steps: Create the resource group and a virtual network with two subnets: az group create -n rg-il28-m41 -l eastus; az network vnet create -g rg-il28-m41 -n vnet-m41 --address-prefix 10.0.0.0/16 --subnet-name aks-subnet --subnet-prefix 10.0.0.0/20; az network vnet subnet create -g rg-il28-m41 --vnet-name vnet-m41 -n appgw-subnet --address-prefix 10.0.16.0/24.

Create the AKS cluster with a system pool only: az aks create -g rg-il28-m41 -n aks-m41 --node-count 3 --node-vm-size Standard_D4s_v5 --vnet-subnet-id <aks-subnet-id> --network-plugin azure. Record the system pool name with az aks nodepool list.

Add a user pool with the autoscaler: az aks nodepool add -g rg-il28-m41 --cluster-name aks-m41 -n apipool --node-count 2 --node-vm-size Standard_D8s_v5 --enable-cluster-autoscaler --min-count 2 --max-count 6.
Get credentials and verify both pools: az aks get-credentials -g rg-il28-m41 -n aks-m41; kubectl get nodes -l agentpool=apipool and kubectl get nodes -l kubernetes.azure.com/mode=system.

Taint the system pool so workloads stay off it: kubectl taint nodes -l kubernetes.azure.com/mode=system CriticalAddonsOnly=true:NoSchedule. Deploy a test pod without tolerations and confirm via kubectl describe that it avoids system nodes.
Deploy AGIC: create the Application Gateway in appgw-subnet, then helm install agic with the gateway ID (follow the current AGIC add-on docs), and verify the ingress controller pod is Running.

Deploy a sample app (two Deployments: web and api, each with a ClusterIP Service) and an Ingress with host shop.local, path /api/* -> api service and /* -> web service, using ingress class azure/application-gateway.
Force a scale-up: temporarily set the api Deployment replicas to 60 with high CPU requests, watch kubectl get pods for Pending, then kubectl get nodes to see the autoscaler add nodes to apipool.
Practice triage: pick one Pending pod, run kubectl describe pod, and write down the FailedScheduling reason; then scale the deployment back to 2 and watch scale-down after ~10 minutes.
Raise the ceiling manually: az aks nodepool update -g rg-il28-m41 --cluster-name aks-m41 -n apipool --max-count 10; confirm with az aks nodepool show.
Clean up to stop charges: az group delete -n rg-il28-m41 --yes --no-wait. Verify deletion with az group show.

Write a one-page triage runbook: the 12-check list for 'new nodes still not deploying' (autoscaler logs, quotas, region capacity, taints, labels, identity permissions, Activity log, Azure Monitor, Resource Health, subnet IPs, SKU restrictions, Azure Policy, max pods).
handsOnLab.deliverable: A running (then deleted) two-pool AKS cluster, a working host/path Ingress through Application Gateway, and a one-page Pending-pod/node-provisioning triage runbook.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: kubectl get nodes shows both pools; the Ingress routes /api/* and /* correctly; your runbook lists all 12 triage checks; the resource group is deleted (az group show returns not found).

mockTask.q: Panel scenario: you raised an AKS node pool's max-count from 6 to 12, pods are still Pending, and no new nodes appear after 10 minutes. What do you check FIRST?
choices: The Azure Activity log for failed VM creation operations and the subscription's vCPU quota
Delete and recreate the node pool
mockTask.explain: No new nodes after a ceiling raise means Azure refused or never received the VM creation. The Activity log shows the failed operation and its error code (quota, policy, SKU capacity); the quota check confirms the most common cause. Restarting autoscaler components or editing pod specs cannot fix a cloud-side denial.

title: AWS Core: VPC, EC2, S3, IAM & EKS
summary: Build AWS fundamentals end to end — VPC networking and triage, EC2 lifecycle and pricing, S3 storage classes, IAM least privilege with real CLI verification, EKS with IRSA, and the ALB-vs-NLB L4/L7 mapping.
objectives: Design a two-tier VPC and triage loss of internet egress using route tables, NAT, security groups, and NACLs
Choose EC2 pricing models and lifecycle actions correctly and predict their billing effects
Apply S3 storage classes and lifecycle policies to match cost with access patterns
Implement least privilege with IAM roles, policy simulation, and zero long-lived keys
Run workloads on EKS with IRSA and choose ALB vs NLB by protocol layer

notes.title: VPC: Your Private Network in AWS
notes.body: A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is an isolated software-defined network you own inside AWS, defined by a CIDR block such as 10.0.0.0/16. Inside it you carve subnets: public subnets whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway, and private subnets whose default route points at a NAT Gateway so instances can reach out (for patches, package downloads) without being reachable inbound. Route tables are the actual routing decisions — a subnet is 'public' only because its route table says so. Security groups are stateful instance-level firewalls (return traffic is automatically allowed); network ACLs are stateless subnet-level filters (you must allow return traffic explicitly). Worked example: an EC2 instance in a private subnet cannot curl https://example.com. Diagnose: (1) route table for the subnet — does 0.0.0.0/0 point to a NAT Gateway in a public subnet? (2) the NAT Gateway itself — is it in a public subnet with an Elastic IP, and is it 'available'? (3) the security group — does it allow outbound HTTPS (default allows all outbound, but a hardened SG may not)? (4) the NACL — stateless, so ephemeral return ports 1024-65535 must be allowed inbound. Solution in most real cases: the NAT Gateway was placed in the private subnet, or the route table points at a deleted NAT Gateway. Fix the route, not the instance.

notes.title: EC2: Instances, Lifecycle, and Pricing Models
notes.body: EC2 provides virtual machines with a lifecycle every operator must know cold: pending -> running -> (reboot keeps the instance; stop/start moves it to new hardware and changes a non-EIP public IP) -> stopped -> terminated. Key instance facts: the AMI defines the OS and preinstalled software; the instance type (e.g. m6i.large) defines vCPU/RAM/network; EBS volumes persist independently of the instance; instance store volumes are ephemeral and vanish on stop. Pricing models map to workload shapes: On-Demand for unpredictable short work, Reserved/Savings Plans for steady 1-3 year baselines, and Spot for fault-tolerant batch at deep discounts with 2-minute interruption warnings. Worked example: a nightly ETL job runs 2 hours on 8 vCPUs and tolerates restarts. Solution: run it on Spot — checkpoint progress to S3 every 15 minutes, handle the interruption notice, and the job costs a fraction of On-Demand. Counter-example: the primary database goes on On-Demand or Reserved, never Spot — an interruption there is an outage, not a retry. The exam-style trap: 'stopped' instances still incur EBS charges; only 'terminated' stops the meter for the instance itself. Always verify state with aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,State.Name]'.

notes.title: S3: Object Storage, Storage Classes, and Consistency
notes.body: S3 stores objects in buckets: flat key/value storage with 11-nines durability design, unlimited scale, and strong read-after-write consistency for all operations. Buckets are global-named but region-resident — pick the region near your compute to avoid cross-region latency and transfer costs. Storage classes trade retrieval cost for storage cost: Standard for hot data, Intelligent-Tiering for unknown patterns, Standard-IA/One Zone-IA for infrequent access, Glacier Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive for backups with minutes-to-hours retrieval. Lifecycle policies automate transitions (e.g. logs -> Standard-IA after 30 days -> Glacier after 90 -> expire after 365). Versioning keeps every overwrite as a new version — your cheapest accidental-deletion insurance. Worked example: application logs, 500 GB/month, rarely read after 7 days, must be retained 1 year for audit. Solution: bucket with lifecycle rule — transition to Standard-IA at 30 days, to Glacier Flexible at 90 days, expire at 365; enable versioning plus MFA delete on the audit prefix. The classic cost mistake is leaving everything in Standard forever; the classic availability mistake is assuming cross-region replication is on by default — it is not, enable CRR explicitly for DR.

notes.title: IAM: Users, Roles, Policies, and Least Privilege
notes.body: IAM is AWS's identity system and the foundation of least privilege: no identity gets permissions it does not need, and permissions shrink over time. Users are long-lived identities (humans, or legacy service accounts); roles are assumed temporarily via STS and are what EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and EKS pods should use — never embed access keys on an instance when an instance profile (role) does the job. Policies are JSON documents with Allow/Deny statements; an explicit Deny always wins. The policy evaluation order to recite in interviews: explicit Deny > explicit Allow > default implicit Deny. Attach policies to groups and roles, not individual users. Worked example: a CI job needs to push images to ECR and nothing else. Bad solution: an IAM user with AdministratorAccess and keys in the pipeline. Correct solution: an IAM role with a policy allowing only ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability, ecr:PutImage, and related push actions on the specific repository ARN, assumed by the CI runner via OIDC federation — no long-lived keys at all. Verify effective permissions before deploying with aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <role-arn> --action-names ecr:PutImage --resource-arns <repo-arn>. Rotate any remaining access keys on a schedule and delete unused ones; keys older than 90 days are an audit finding.

notes.title: EKS and the Kubernetes-on-AWS Map
notes.body: EKS is AWS's managed Kubernetes: AWS runs the control plane (API server, etcd) across multiple AZs while you own the worker nodes (managed node groups, Fargate profiles, or self-managed). The concepts from AKS transfer directly: node groups are the EKS analogue of node pools, the cluster autoscaler works the same way, and IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) map Kubernetes service accounts to IAM roles — the AWS-native answer to workload identity. Networking: pods run in your VPC (VPC CNI assigns VPC IPs, so subnet sizing matters exactly as with Azure CNI), and exposure uses either an Application/Network Load Balancer via the AWS Load Balancer Controller or an Ingress resource. Worked example: a pod needs to read from S3. Anti-pattern: baking AWS keys into the container image. Solution: create an IAM role with s3:GetObject on the bucket, annotate the Kubernetes service account with eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn, and the pod's AWS SDK calls assume the role automatically via the projected OIDC token — no secrets to rotate. EKS vs AKS vs GKE in one line each: EKS leans on IAM/IRSA and VPC CNI; AKS leans on Azure AD workload identity and Azure CNI; GKE leans on Workload Identity and alias IPs. The control plane is managed in all three; your job is nodes, networking, and identity in all three.

notes.title: ALB vs NLB: The L4/L7 Lesson, AWS Edition
notes.body: This is the AWS retelling of the App Gateway vs Load Balancer distinction, and panels love the mapping. The Network Load Balancer (NLB) operates at Layer 4: it forwards TCP/UDP (and TLS passthrough) with ultra-low latency and static IPs, preserving the client source IP — the right choice for gaming, VoIP, or any non-HTTP protocol. The Application Load Balancer (ALB) operates at Layer 7: it understands HTTP/HTTPS, routes by host header and path, terminates TLS, and integrates with WAF — the right choice for web APIs and microservices, and the natural target of a Kubernetes Ingress via the AWS Load Balancer Controller. Worked example: expose payments.example.com/api to the payments service and payments.example.com/ to the storefront, both TLS-terminated with WAF. Solution: one ALB with two listener rules — host+path condition /api/* -> payments target group, default -> storefront target group, ACM certificate on the HTTPS listener, WAF ACL associated. The trap: choosing NLB for HTTP routing because 'it is faster' — you then reimplement path routing in every service. And the cost trap: an ALB per microservice instead of one ALB with path rules multiplies the hourly charge by the service count. One ALB, many rules; NLB only when the protocol is not HTTP.

cards.front: What makes a subnet 'public' in AWS?
cards.back: Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway — the label is a consequence of routing, not a property of the subnet

cards.front: Security group vs network ACL (stateful vs stateless)
cards.back: Security groups are stateful (return traffic auto-allowed) at the instance/ENI level; NACLs are stateless at the subnet level — you must explicitly allow return ephemeral ports

cards.front: EC2 stop vs terminate (billing + behavior)
cards.back: Stop: instance halts, EBS persists and still bills, public IP may change on start. Terminate: instance deleted; EBS bills until volumes are deleted too

cards.front: AWS CLI: list instance IDs and states
cards.back: aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,State.Name]' --output table

cards.front: S3 storage class for logs rarely read after a week, kept 1 year
cards.back: Lifecycle policy: Standard -> Standard-IA (30d) -> Glacier Flexible (90d) -> expire (365d); enable versioning for the audit prefix

cards.front: IAM policy evaluation order
cards.back: Explicit Deny beats explicit Allow beats implicit (default) Deny

cards.front: How should an EC2 instance or pod get AWS permissions? (no keys)
cards.back: Assume an IAM role: instance profile for EC2, IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) for EKS pods via OIDC

cards.front: AWS CLI: test whether a role can push to ECR before deploying
cards.back: aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <role> --action-names ecr:PutImage --resource-arns <repo>

cards.front: EKS analogue of an AKS node pool
cards.back: Managed node group (plus Fargate profiles); cluster autoscaler and IRSA map 1:1 from AKS concepts

cards.front: ALB vs NLB in one line each
cards.back: ALB = Layer 7: HTTP host/path routing, TLS termination, WAF. NLB = Layer 4: TCP/UDP, ultra-low latency, static IP, preserves source IP

cards.front: Why not one ALB per microservice?
cards.back: Each ALB bills hourly — use one ALB with host/path listener rules fanning out to many target groups

cards.front: VPC CNI IP planning gotcha (mirrors Azure CNI)
cards.back: Pods consume real VPC IPs, so subnets must be sized for max pods; exhaustion blocks scheduling and node joins

quiz.q: An EC2 instance in a private subnet cannot reach the internet. The NAT Gateway exists and is 'available'. What do you check FIRST?
choices: The subnet's route table: does 0.0.0.0/0 point to that NAT Gateway?
quiz.explain: Outbound routing is decided by the route table. A NAT Gateway in the wrong subnet or a route pointing at a deleted gateway are the classic causes; CPU credits are irrelevant to networking.

quiz.q: A security group allows inbound 443 but the app still fails. The NACL is custom. What is the likely NACL mistake?
choices: The stateless NACL does not allow the ephemeral return ports (1024-65535) inbound
NACLs only apply to public subnets
quiz.explain: NACLs are stateless: the HTTPS response returns on ephemeral ports, which must be explicitly allowed inbound. Security groups are stateful and handle this automatically.

quiz.q: Which EC2 pricing model fits a fault-tolerant 2-hour nightly ETL that checkpoints to S3?
choices: Reserved for 3 years with no checkpointing
quiz.explain: Spot gives deep discounts for interruptible work; checkpointing to S3 makes the 2-minute interruption warning survivable. Databases and steady baselines do not belong on Spot.

quiz.q: A stopped EC2 instance is still generating charges. Why?
choices: AWS bills stopped instances at full price
Attached EBS volumes keep billing until deleted
quiz.explain: Stopping halts the instance meter, but EBS volumes persist and bill independently. Only deleting the volumes (or terminating with delete-on-termination) stops storage charges.

quiz.q: 500 GB/month of logs, rarely read after 7 days, 1-year retention required. Best S3 design?
choices: Lifecycle: Standard-IA at 30 days, Glacier Flexible at 90 days, expire at 365 days, versioning on
One Zone-IA for everything with no expiry
quiz.explain: Lifecycle transitions match cost to access pattern; expiry enforces retention; versioning protects the audit trail. Standard forever is the classic cost mistake.

quiz.q: A CI pipeline needs to push images to one ECR repo. Most secure design?
choices: IAM user with AdministratorAccess, keys in pipeline variables
IAM role assumable via OIDC with a policy allowing only ECR push actions on that repo ARN
Public ECR repo with no auth
quiz.explain: OIDC-assumed roles eliminate long-lived keys entirely, and scoping to push-only actions on one ARN is least privilege. Admin keys in CI are a breach waiting to happen.

quiz.q: In IAM, a policy Allows s3:* and another attached policy Denies s3:DeleteBucket. Can the identity delete the bucket?
choices: Yes, the most recent policy wins
quiz.explain: Explicit Deny overrides any Allow. Evaluation order: explicit Deny > explicit Allow > implicit Deny.

quiz.q: An EKS pod needs read access to one S3 bucket. Correct approach?
choices: Bake AWS access keys into the container image
IRSA: IAM role with s3:GetObject on the bucket, mapped to the pod's service account via OIDC annotation
Open the bucket to the public
SSH into the node and configure the AWS CLI
quiz.explain: IRSA gives the pod short-lived credentials for exactly one role with no keys to rotate or leak. Keys in images end up in registries and git history.

quiz.q: You need host/path routing with TLS termination and WAF for HTTP microservices on AWS. Which load balancer?
quiz.explain: ALB is Layer 7: host/path rules, TLS termination, WAF integration. NLB is Layer 4 for TCP/UDP; it cannot do HTTP routing.

drills.title: Timed drill: VPC and EC2 triage

items.prompt: 60 seconds: private-subnet instance cannot reach the internet. Your 4 checks in order?
items.answer: Route table 0.0.0.0/0 -> NAT GW; NAT GW in public subnet + available; security group outbound; NACL ephemeral return ports.
items.explain: Routing first, then the gateway's own placement, then stateful SG, then stateless NACL. Say it in this order.

items.prompt: What single route-table fact makes a subnet public?
items.answer: A route sending 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway.
items.explain: 'Public' is a routing property, not a subnet property — the panel wants this exact framing.

items.prompt: Stateful vs stateless: which is the security group, which the NACL?
items.answer: Security group = stateful (return auto-allowed). NACL = stateless (explicit both directions).
items.explain: This distinction explains every 'SG allows it but traffic still fails' mystery.

items.prompt: Command: list all EC2 instance IDs with their states in a table.
items.answer: aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,State.Name]' --output table
items.explain: JMESPath query keeps it to the two fields you need during triage.

items.prompt: Stop vs terminate: what keeps billing after each?
items.answer: Stop: EBS volumes keep billing. Terminate: nothing, once volumes are deleted.
items.explain: The instance meter stops on stop; the storage meter does not.

items.prompt: Spot vs On-Demand: which for the primary database, and why?
items.answer: On-Demand (or Reserved). Spot interruptions are fine for checkpointed batch, never for a database.
items.explain: Match pricing to interruptibility — say the 2-minute warning and who can tolerate it.

items.prompt: S3: name the storage classes for hot, unknown-pattern, and archival data.
items.answer: Hot: Standard. Unknown: Intelligent-Tiering. Archive: Glacier Flexible/Deep Archive.
items.explain: Three buckets of the lifecycle: hot, unknown, cold — with lifecycle policies automating the transitions.

drills.title: Timed drill: IAM and least privilege

items.prompt: Recite the IAM policy evaluation order.
items.answer: Explicit Deny > explicit Allow > implicit (default) Deny.
items.explain: One line, no hesitation — panels use it as a warm-up check.

items.prompt: EC2 instance needs S3 read. Keys on the instance or instance profile?
items.answer: Instance profile (IAM role). Never long-lived keys on compute.
items.explain: Roles give short-lived credentials automatically; keys get leaked, forgotten, and never rotated.

items.prompt: Command: simulate whether a role can ecr:PutImage on a repo.
items.answer: aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <role-arn> --action-names ecr:PutImage --resource-arns <repo-arn>
items.explain: Simulate before deploying — it evaluates the real policy set without making the call.

items.prompt: EKS pod needs S3 access. Name the mechanism and the annotation.
items.answer: IRSA — annotate the ServiceAccount with eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn.
items.explain: IAM Roles for Service Accounts: OIDC-projected token, role assumption, no secrets.

items.prompt: CI pushes to one ECR repo. Scope the policy.
items.answer: Allow only ECR push actions (GetAuthorizationToken, BatchCheckLayerAvailability, PutImage, Initiate/UploadPart/CompleteLayerUpload) on that repo ARN.
items.explain: Name the actions and the ARN scope — 'ECR full access' fails the least-privilege question.

items.prompt: ALB vs NLB: which terminates TLS and does path routing?
items.answer: ALB (Layer 7). NLB is Layer 4 TCP/UDP passthrough.
items.explain: Map to Azure: ALB ~ Application Gateway, NLB ~ Azure Load Balancer.

items.prompt: Cost trap: one ALB per microservice. Fix?
items.answer: One ALB with host/path listener rules to many target groups.
items.explain: ALBs bill hourly each — fan out with rules, not with load balancers.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: VPC, least-privilege IAM, and EKS with IRSA
handsOnLab.brief: You will build a two-tier VPC, launch an EC2 instance in the private tier, create a least-privilege IAM role, stand up a small EKS cluster, and give a pod S3 access through IRSA with no long-lived keys. Tear everything down at the end; expect a few dollars of charges if completed same-day.
steps: Create the VPC and tiers: aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.1.0.0/16; create public subnet 10.1.1.0/24 and private subnet 10.1.2.0/24 in the same AZ; create and attach an Internet Gateway; add 0.0.0.0/0 -> IGW on the public route table.
Create a NAT Gateway with an Elastic IP in the public subnet; add 0.0.0.0/0 -> NAT Gateway on the private route table. Verify with aws ec2 describe-route-tables.

Launch an Amazon Linux EC2 instance in the private subnet with no public IP and an instance profile role allowing only s3:GetObject on one bucket; SSH via Session Manager and curl https://example.com to prove NAT egress works.
Create an S3 bucket with versioning enabled; write a lifecycle rule (console or CLI) moving objects to Standard-IA after 30 days; upload a test object and confirm aws s3 ls shows it.
Draft the CI deployer policy: JSON allowing only ECR push actions on one repository ARN; run aws iam simulate-principal-policy against it for ecr:PutImage (expect allowed) and iam:* (expect denied).

Create the EKS cluster: eksctl create cluster --name il28-m42 --region us-east-1 --nodegroup-name workers --node-type t3.medium --nodes 2 --nodes-min 1 --nodes-max 4 (or the equivalent aws eks create-cluster + nodegroup commands).
Create an IAM role for IRSA with s3:GetObject on your bucket; associate the OIDC provider; annotate a Kubernetes ServiceAccount with eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn.
Deploy a test pod using that ServiceAccount that runs aws s3 ls s3://<bucket>; confirm it lists objects with no keys present in the pod (env | grep AWS shows nothing).
Expose the pod via an Ingress and the AWS Load Balancer Controller: confirm an ALB is provisioned and routes by path to your service.
Document the ALB-vs-NLB decision for three workloads (public REST API, game voice chat UDP, internal TCP service) in your lab notes.
Delete in order: eksctl delete cluster, NAT Gateway + Elastic IP release, EC2 termination, VPC deletion; verify with aws ec2 describe-vpcs that nothing remains.
Write the one-page incident note: 'private instance lost internet' with the 4-check triage from the drill.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A (then deleted) VPC with public/private tiers, a least-privilege IAM role validated by simulation, an EKS cluster where a pod reads S3 via IRSA with zero keys, and an ALB-vs-NLB decision note.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: curl from the private instance succeeds; the pod lists S3 objects with no AWS keys in its env; aws ec2 describe-vpcs shows the lab VPC gone after teardown.

mockTask.q: Your EKS pods need to read objects from one S3 bucket. A teammate proposes baking an IAM user's access keys into the container image 'because it is simple'. What do you do?
choices: Use IRSA: an IAM role scoped to s3:GetObject on that bucket, mapped to the pod's ServiceAccount via OIDC
Make the bucket public and skip IAM
Put the keys in a ConfigMap instead
mockTask.explain: IRSA issues short-lived credentials scoped to one role with no keys to rotate, leak, or commit. Keys in images end up in registries and layer history; ConfigMaps are not secret storage; public buckets are a breach.

title: GCP Core: Compute, GKE & IAM
summary: Master Google Cloud's project hierarchy, global VPCs, Compute Engine, GKE Standard vs Autopilot, Cloud IAM, and Cloud Storage — with a full AWS/Azure/GCP compare-and-contrast sheet for panel questions.
objectives: Navigate the GCP resource hierarchy and isolate environments with projects and named gcloud configurations
Build custom-mode VPCs and debug firewall rules through tag bindings
Run Compute Engine VMs cost-effectively with preemptibles and committed-use reasoning
Deploy GKE in Standard and Autopilot modes and grant pods storage access via Workload Identity
Map every AWS/Azure primitive from M41-M42 to its GCP equivalent for cross-cloud panel questions

notes.title: Projects and the Resource Hierarchy
notes.body: Everything in Google Cloud lives under a project, and projects nest under folders and an organization node. This hierarchy is not cosmetic: IAM policies and organization policies inherit downward, so a deny on the organization applies to every project beneath it. One project typically maps to one environment or application (billing-project-dev, billing-project-prod), which gives you per-project billing breakdowns and blast-radius isolation for free. Quotas are enforced per project per region — the GCP analogue of the Azure subscription quota you triaged in M41. The gcloud CLI scopes every command to a project: gcloud config set project my-proj, or per-command with --project. Worked example: a developer's gcloud compute instances list returns instances from the wrong environment. Diagnosis: gcloud config list shows core/project set to the prod project. Solution: gcloud config set project billing-project-dev, or better, use named configurations — gcloud config configurations create dev && gcloud config configurations activate dev — so switching environments is one command instead of editing config each time. The interview point: GCP's project model makes environment separation structural, where AWS leans on accounts and Azure on subscriptions/resource groups.

notes.title: VPC Networks and Firewall Rules
notes.body: A GCP VPC is global by default: one VPC spans all regions, and subnets are regional slices of it. This differs from AWS, where a VPC is regional and you peer across regions. Subnets have two modes: auto (a subnet per region created for you — fine for experiments, never for production) and custom (you define every subnet's CIDR — the production choice). Firewall rules in GCP are stateful and VPC-scoped, applied by tags or service accounts: e.g. allow tcp:443 from 0.0.0.0/0 to instances tagged web. There are no NACLs — one less layer than AWS. Implied rules exist: allow all egress, deny all ingress; your rules punch holes in the ingress deny. Worked example: a Compute Engine VM tagged 'api' serves nothing on port 8080 despite the app listening. Diagnosis: gcloud compute firewall-rules list shows no rule targeting tag 'api' for tcp:8080. Solution: gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-api-8080 --allow tcp:8080 --target-tags api --source-ranges 10.0.0.0/8. Verify with gcloud compute firewall-rules describe allow-api-8080. The trap: creating the rule with --target-tags web while the instance is tagged api — the rule exists, matches nothing, and the firewall silently drops traffic. Always check the tag binding, not just the rule's existence.

notes.title: Compute Engine: VMs, Images, and Preemptibles
notes.body: Compute Engine VMs are built from images (public, custom, or machine images that bundle disks), shaped by machine types (e2-standard-4, n2, c2 for compute-heavy), and billed per second. Disks are persistent by default and independent of the VM, mirroring EBS semantics. Two GCP-specific concepts matter. First, preemptible VMs: up to deep discounts, terminable by Google with 30 seconds' notice — the GCP analogue of Spot, ideal for the same checkpointed batch work. Second, committed use discounts: 1- or 3-year commitments on steady capacity, the analogue of Reserved Instances/Savings Plans. Live migration keeps most VMs running through host maintenance, so reboots for maintenance are rarer than on other clouds. Worked example: list all running VMs across zones with their machine types: gcloud compute instances list --filter='status=RUNNING' --format='table(name,zone,machineType)'. To stop paying for an idle dev VM but keep its disk: gcloud compute instances stop my-dev-vm --zone us-central1-a — the disk persists and bills, the VM does not. The cost trap mirrors AWS: stopping is not deleting; disks, static IPs, and load balancer forwarding rules all bill independently. Audit monthly with gcloud compute disks list --filter='-users:*' to find orphaned disks.

notes.title: GKE: Standard vs Autopilot
notes.body: Google Kubernetes Engine comes in two modes. Standard mode: you manage the node pools (the direct analogue of AKS node pools and EKS node groups), choose machine types, and run the cluster autoscaler yourself. Autopilot: Google manages nodes, scaling, and security hardening — you declare workloads and pay per pod-requested resources, trading control for operational simplicity. Autopilot enforces opinions: no privileged pods, required resource requests, restricted host access. Workload Identity is GKE's IRSA equivalent: bind a Kubernetes ServiceAccount to a Google service account and pods get short-lived tokens with no keys — gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding with the workloadIdentityUser role. Worked example: create a standard cluster with two node pools: gcloud container clusters create il28-m43 --zone us-central1-a --machine-type e2-standard-4 --num-nodes 3, then gcloud container node-pools create batchpool --cluster il28-m43 --machine-type e2-standard-8 --preemptible --num-nodes 0 --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes 0 --max-nodes 10. The preemptible batch pool at min 0 mirrors the AKS spot-pool pattern from M41 exactly. The interview mapping to recite: node pools (AKS) = managed node groups (EKS) = node pools (GKE Standard); workload identity (AKS) = IRSA (EKS) = Workload Identity (GKE).

notes.title: Cloud IAM: Members, Roles, and Deny Policies
notes.body: Cloud IAM grants roles to members (users, groups, service accounts, domains) on resources, and permissions inherit down the hierarchy. Roles come in three flavors: basic (Owner/Editor/Viewer — broad, avoid in production), predefined (e.g. roles/compute.viewer — least-privilege friendly), and custom (your own permission sets). Service accounts are the non-human identities: every Compute Engine VM and every CI job should act as a service account, never as a user key — gcloud iam service-accounts keys create is the command you should almost never run, because keys are the leak vector. Prefer impersonation and workload identity federation instead. Deny policies (organization-level) let you write explicit denys, the GCP answer to AWS's explicit-Deny-wins rule. Worked example: a deploy service account needs to push images to Artifact Registry and nothing else. Solution: grant roles/artifactregistry.writer on the specific repository resource to the service account — not Editor on the project. Verify with gcloud projects get-iam-policy to audit bindings. The panel-ready contrast with AWS IAM: GCP binds roles to members per resource with inheritance; AWS attaches policies to users/groups/roles with explicit-Deny precedence. Both converge on the same practice: predefined narrow roles, service accounts for machines, no long-lived keys.

notes.title: Cloud Storage Classes and Lifecycle
notes.body: Cloud Storage buckets hold objects with the same four-class pattern as S3: Standard (hot), Nearline (read less than monthly), Coldline (read less than quarterly), Archive (yearly or less) — each step down cuts storage cost and raises retrieval cost and minimum durations (30/90/365 days). Autoclass automates transitions for unpredictable patterns, the analogue of S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Lifecycle rules in JSON transition or delete objects by age, and Object Versioning plus retention policies protect audit data. Buckets are global-named like S3; use gsutil or gcloud storage (the newer CLI): gcloud storage buckets create gs://my-bucket --location=us-central1 --storage-class=STANDARD. Worked example: the same 500 GB/month logs from M42, rarely read after a week, 1-year retention. Solution: lifecycle rule — SetStorageClass to NEARLINE at 30 days, to COLDLINE at 90 days, Delete at 365 days; enable versioning on the audit prefix. Verify: gcloud storage buckets describe gs://my-bucket --format=json | grep lifecycle. The cross-cloud trap: minimum storage durations — moving an object to Archive and deleting it at day 40 still bills 365 days. Lifecycle design must respect minimums or the 'savings' become a surcharge.

notes.title: Azure vs AWS vs GCP: The Compare-and-Contrast Sheet
notes.body: Panels ask you to compare clouds, so carry this sheet. Networking: AWS VPC is regional with IGW/NAT and SG+NACL; Azure VNet is regional with NSGs and route tables; GCP VPC is global with regional subnets and stateful firewall rules only. Identity: AWS IAM (users/roles/policies, explicit deny wins), Azure RBAC + Microsoft Entra (role assignments on scopes), GCP Cloud IAM (members/roles/resources with inheritance, deny policies). Compute: EC2 / Azure VMs / Compute Engine — all per-second billing, all with interruptible discounts (Spot / Spot VMs / preemptible). Kubernetes: EKS / AKS / GKE — managed control planes; node pools in all three; workload identity via IRSA / workload identity / Workload Identity. Object storage: S3 / Blob / Cloud Storage — hot-to-archive tiers with lifecycle automation in all three. The strategic point for M44: the primitives are 90% interchangeable, which is why Terraform can abstract them — the remaining 10% (IAM models, networking defaults, identity federation) is where multicloud gets expensive. Worked example: map the M42 lab to GCP — VPC becomes a custom-mode global VPC, the NAT Gateway becomes Cloud NAT, the IAM role becomes a service account with a predefined role, EKS+IRSA becomes GKE+Workload Identity, ALB becomes a global external HTTP(S) load balancer. If you can narrate that mapping, you can work on any cloud.

cards.front: GCP resource hierarchy order (top to bottom)
cards.back: Organization -> folders -> projects -> resources; IAM and organization policies inherit downward

cards.front: How do you switch gcloud between dev and prod cleanly?
cards.back: Named configurations: gcloud config configurations create dev / activate dev — never hand-edit core/project per command

cards.front: GCP VPC: global or regional? Subnets?
cards.back: VPC is global; subnets are regional. (AWS VPCs are regional.) Use custom subnet mode in production, never auto mode

cards.front: GCP firewall rule targeting gotcha
cards.back: Rules bind via --target-tags or service accounts; a rule with the wrong tag matches nothing and traffic is silently dropped. Check the binding, not just the rule

cards.front: Command: create a firewall rule for tcp:8080 to instances tagged 'api'
cards.back: gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-api-8080 --allow tcp:8080 --target-tags api --source-ranges 10.0.0.0/8

cards.front: GCP's analogue of AWS Spot instances
cards.back: Preemptible VMs — deep discount, 30-second termination notice; use for checkpointed batch, never for databases

cards.front: GKE Standard vs Autopilot
cards.back: Standard: you manage node pools, machine types, autoscaler. Autopilot: Google manages nodes/security; you pay per pod requests; privileged pods restricted

cards.front: GKE's equivalent of EKS IRSA
cards.back: Workload Identity: bind a Kubernetes ServiceAccount to a Google service account; pods get short-lived tokens, no keys

cards.front: Command you should almost never run (GCP keys)
cards.back: gcloud iam service-accounts keys create — long-lived keys are the leak vector; use impersonation or workload identity federation

cards.front: Cloud Storage classes in access-frequency order
cards.back: Standard -> Nearline (monthly) -> Coldline (quarterly) -> Archive (yearly); minimum durations 30/90/365 days

cards.front: Cross-cloud identity mapping (one line)
cards.back: EKS IRSA = AKS workload identity = GKE Workload Identity: short-lived tokens mapping K8s service accounts to cloud roles

cards.front: The 90/10 multicloud summary
cards.back: Primitives are ~90% interchangeable (Terraform abstracts them); the costly 10% is IAM models, networking defaults, and identity federation

quiz.q: A gcloud command lists instances from the wrong environment. Fastest correct fix?
choices: gcloud config configurations activate dev (use named configurations per environment)
quiz.explain: The active configuration's core/project selects the project. Named configurations make environment switching one command and prevent prod/dev mix-ups.

quiz.q: Why is a GCP VPC described as global while an AWS VPC is regional?
choices: One GCP VPC spans all regions with regional subnets; AWS VPCs live in one region and peer across regions
quiz.explain: GCP VPCs are global constructs; subnets are the regional slices. AWS VPCs are regional, so cross-region traffic needs peering or Transit Gateway.

quiz.q: A firewall rule allows tcp:8080 with --target-tags web, but the VM is tagged api and serves nothing. Cause?
choices: The rule's target tag does not match the VM's tag, so the rule matches nothing
quiz.explain: Tag binding is exact: the rule exists but selects zero instances. Always verify the target binding, not just the rule's existence.

quiz.q: Which workload belongs on preemptible VMs?
choices: A checkpointed nightly batch job that tolerates restarts
A stateful message queue with no replication

title: Multicloud Strategy & Comparison
summary: Make deliberate cloud decisions: a five-lens selection framework, Terraform as the neutral control plane, data-gravity and egress economics, regulatory constraints, and the platform-team operating model that makes multicloud survivable.
objectives: Apply the five-lens framework to choose a cloud per workload with written reasons
Design Terraform modules with a common interface across providers and test parity in CI
Reason about data gravity and egress economics in architecture decisions
Apply residency, sovereignty, and audit controls to financial-services workloads
Define the platform-team operating model that contains multicloud cognitive cost

notes.title: When to Use Which Cloud: A Decision Framework
notes.body: Choose a cloud per workload, not per fashion. The framework has five lenses. (1) Service fit: each cloud leads somewhere — if your data warehouse and analytics gravity is BigQuery, GCP pulls; if your enterprise identity is Microsoft Entra and your apps are .NET, Azure pulls; if you need the broadest service catalog and region count, AWS pulls. (2) Team skill: a team fluent in ARM/Bicep and Azure networking will ship faster on Azure than relearning IAM and VPCs under deadline. (3) Commercial terms: existing enterprise agreements, committed-use discounts, and credits can outweigh technical preferences. (4) Latency and residency: users and regulators pin regions; the cloud with the right region wins regardless of features. (5) Exit cost: managed services with proprietary APIs (the serverless and AI offerings especially) raise switching costs; VMs and Kubernetes keep you portable. Worked example: a .NET shop on Entra with a new Python analytics workload. Solution: keep the .NET estate on Azure (identity and skill fit), but evaluate the analytics workload independently — if it is mostly BigQuery-shaped, a deliberate two-cloud footprint with Terraform managing both beats forcing analytics onto the wrong platform. The anti-pattern is 'we are a single-cloud shop' as dogma, and equally 'every team picks its own cloud' as anarchy — the framework forces a written reason per workload.

notes.title: Terraform as the Cloud-Agnostic Control Plane
notes.body: Terraform is the closest thing to a neutral control plane: one language, one state model, one plan/apply workflow across providers. The portability is real but partial, and panels probe the boundary. What transfers: resource lifecycle thinking, module composition, for_each patterns, state management, and CI-driven applies. What does not transfer: provider schemas (an azurerm_virtual_network and an aws_vpc share nothing but the concept), IAM models (role assignments vs policies vs bindings), and identity federation for the pipeline itself. The professional pattern is a thin provider-specific module per cloud exposing a common interface: module 'network' with inputs like cidr_block and outputs like subnet_ids, implemented once per cloud. Worked example: provision a two-tier network on both Azure and AWS from one root module. Solution sketch: root module calls module/network-azure and module/network-aws, each wrapping the native resources; shared locals define the CIDR plan once; outputs converge to subnet IDs consumed identically downstream. The trap: writing 'cloud-agnostic' HCL that secretly depends on one provider's defaults (e.g. assuming AWS-style security groups exist on Azure) — abstraction without testing is fiction. Test every module against every provider it claims to support, in CI, on every change.

notes.title: Case Study (Hypothetical): A Large Bank Standardizes on One Primary Cloud
notes.body: Exercise — hypothetical, no claims about any real institution: a large bank with 40,000 employees decides to standardize on one primary cloud while keeping a second for specific workloads. Walk the decision the way a panel wants to hear it. Drivers for standardizing: one identity model for auditors, one network architecture for the security team to certify, one skill ladder for hiring, volume pricing on commits, and a single incident-response playbook. Drivers for keeping the second cloud: a trading analytics team already productive on its data platform, a regulator requiring in-country processing where only one cloud has the region, and acquisition targets running elsewhere. The decision output is not 'Azure' or 'AWS' — it is a written cloud strategy: primary cloud for 80% of workloads, approved exceptions with sunset reviews, Terraform modules for both, and a landing-zone per cloud with identical guardrails (policy, logging, identity). The interview answer the panel wants: 'Standardize the operating model, not necessarily the provider; make exceptions explicit, reviewed, and temporary.' The failure mode is shadow multicloud — teams adopting a second cloud without the security team knowing, which is how breaches and surprise bills happen. Governance first, provider second.

notes.title: Data Gravity and Egress Economics
notes.body: Data has gravity: the larger the dataset and the more services touch it, the harder it is to move, and every cloud bills for data leaving its network. The economics are qualitative but decisive: ingress is generally free, egress and cross-region transfer are metered, and moving a multi-terabyte warehouse between clouds can cost more than a year of compute. Design consequences: keep compute next to data (same region, ideally same cloud); replicate only what DR truly requires and compress before transfer; prefer private connectivity (ExpressRoute, Direct Connect, Interconnect) for steady high-volume flows over the public internet. Worked example: a 50 TB analytics dataset queried daily by dashboards, with a proposal to run the dashboards' compute on a different cloud 'because the BI tool is nicer there'. Analysis: every dashboard refresh would pull data across clouds over metered egress, and the BI tool would need a full replica to be usable — the 'nicer tool' premium is dwarfed by transfer costs and replica management. Solution: run the BI compute in the same cloud and region as the data, or formally cost the replica plus egress before deciding. The panel one-liner: 'Data gravity decides the cloud; compute follows the data, not the other way around.'

notes.title: Regulatory, Residency, and Sovereignty Constraints
notes.body: Regulators and contracts constrain cloud choice more than engineers like to admit. Financial services face requirements around data residency (customer data stays in-country), audit access (regulators can inspect), operational resilience (survive a provider outage), and increasingly sovereignty (data under domestic legal control). The practical toolkit: region selection with in-country regions, customer-managed keys (CMK/BYOK) so the provider cannot read data at rest without your key, private connectivity instead of public endpoints, and contractual terms covering audit rights and exit assistance. Worked example: a payments workload must keep cardholder data in-country and survive a cloud region failure. Solution: primary deployment in the in-country region with CMK-encrypted storage, private endpoints (Private Link / Private Service Connect) so traffic never traverses the public internet, and a tested failover to a second in-country region — with the failover's data residency verified, not assumed. The trap: assuming 'the cloud is compliant' — compliance is a property of your architecture plus the provider's attestations, never of the provider alone. You inherit the audit burden for everything you configure.

notes.title: Operating Model: The Hidden Cost of Multicloud
notes.body: The dominant cost of multicloud is cognitive, not metered: every additional cloud multiplies the runbooks, IAM models, network designs, incident playbooks, and hiring profiles your platform team must master. A team that is expert in one cloud and novice in two ships slower and incidents worse on all three. The operating-model decision therefore precedes the provider decision: will you run a central platform team (one paved road, opinionated modules, self-service), embedded product teams (each owns its cloud footprint), or a hybrid? The central platform team is the enterprise answer: it publishes Terraform modules, enforces policy, and absorbs the multicloud complexity so product teams see one interface. Worked example: three product teams each built their own networking on three clouds; an incident requires correlating logs across all three at 3 AM. Solution going forward: the platform team publishes one 'landing zone' module per approved cloud with identical guardrails — logging to the central SIEM, identity via the corporate IdP, policy denying public storage — and product teams may only deploy through it. New clouds require platform-team certification first. The panel answer: 'Multicloud without a platform team is just three separate clouds with three times the toil.'

notes.title: Prometheus: The Pull Model and Metric Types
notes.body: Prometheus monitors by scraping: it pulls metrics from HTTP endpoints (usually /metrics) on a fixed interval, storing timestamped samples in its time-series database. Pull inverts the usual push assumption and buys you three things: targets can die without losing the monitoring path's knowledge of them (failed scrapes are themselves a signal via the 'up' metric), service discovery (Kubernetes, EC2, DNS) keeps the target list fresh automatically, and exporters are dumb text endpoints — any app can expose metrics with a client library. Four metric types: Counter (monotonically increasing: http_requests_total), Gauge (goes up and down: memory usage, queue depth), Histogram (observations bucketed for latency quantiles), Summary (precomputed quantiles, less flexible). Worked example: your API exposes http_requests_total{method,code} and http_request_duration_seconds_bucket. Which type answers 'requests per second'? Solution: a Counter — rate(http_requests_total[5m]). Which answers 'current queue depth'? A Gauge — read directly. Which answers 'p99 latency'? The Histogram — histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])). The classic mistake is rate() on a Gauge (meaningless — gauges are not cumulative) or averaging a Counter directly (use rate first).

notes.title: PromQL Basics: rate, increase, and histogram_quantile
notes.body: PromQL is Prometheus's query language; a handful of functions covers most operational questions. rate(v range-vector[5m]) gives per-second average increase — the standard way to read counters. increase() gives the total increase over the window. sum by (label) aggregates: sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])). avg_over_time, max_over_time smooth gauges. histogram_quantile(0.99, ...) computes the p99 from histogram buckets. Alert expressions combine these with thresholds: rate(http_requests_total{code=~'5..'}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.05 fires when the 5xx ratio exceeds 5%. Worked example: 'Is checkout slower than yesterday?' Solution: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route='/checkout'}[5m]))) and compare against the same query with a 24h offset modifier. Second: 'Which pod is OOMKilled most?' — increase(kube_pod_container_status_terminated_reason{reason='OOMKilled'}[1h]) sorted by pod. The trap: rate() needs at least two samples in the window — on a 30s scrape interval, a [1m] window is fragile; use [5m] for stability. And remember counters reset on restart — rate() handles resets, but naive subtraction does not.

notes.title: Grafana: Dashboards That Answer Questions
notes.body: Grafana turns Prometheus (and other sources) into dashboards, but a dashboard is only as good as the questions it answers. Design by the RED method per service — Rate (requests/sec), Errors (error ratio), Duration (latency quantiles) — plus the USE method per resource — Utilization, Saturation, Errors. One row per service with its RED panels; one row per dependency (database, queue) with USE panels. Variables make dashboards reusable: a $namespace or $service dropdown templating every query. Annotations mark deploys so you can correlate a latency spike with the release that caused it. Worked example: build the checkout dashboard. Panels: (1) rate of checkouts: sum(rate(checkout_completed_total[5m])); (2) error ratio: 5xx rate / total rate with a 1% alert threshold line; (3) p50/p95/p99 latency via histogram_quantile; (4) saturation: container CPU throttling rate and memory working set vs limit. Solution review: each panel maps to RED; variables let the same dashboard serve every service; the deploy annotation answers 'what changed?' in one glance. The anti-pattern is the wall of 40 graphs nobody reads — if a panel has never triggered a decision, delete it. Dashboards are operational tools, not art.

notes.title: Centralized Logging: The EFK Pipeline
notes.body: Metrics tell you something is wrong; logs tell you why. The EFK stack — Elasticsearch, Fluent Bit/Fluentd, Kibana (or OpenSearch equivalents) — centralizes logs because containers are ephemeral: when a pod dies, its local logs die with it. The pipeline: application writes structured JSON logs to stdout; the node agent (Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet) tails container logs, parses and enriches them (adds pod, namespace, node labels), and ships to Elasticsearch; Kibana queries and visualizes. Structured logging is the prerequisite — log {timestamp, level, service, trace_id, message, fields} as JSON, never free text, so every field is filterable. Worked example: checkout errors spike; find the cause. Solution: in Kibana, filter level=error AND service=checkout over the spike window, aggregate by fields.error_code — one code dominates; expand a sample document, copy its trace_id, pivot to the trace view to see the failing downstream call. The cost trap is log volume: debug logging in production at millions of transactions per second will bankrupt your Elasticsearch cluster. Set levels per environment (info in prod, debug in dev), sample high-volume access logs, and set index retention (hot 7 days, warm 30, delete after 90) before the disk fills.

notes.title: Azure Monitor: The Native Mapping
notes.body: On Azure, the native observability stack is Azure Monitor: metrics flow into Metrics Explorer, logs into Log Analytics workspaces queried with KQL, and Application Insights provides APM (distributed traces, dependency maps) for applications. Container Insights onboards AKS clusters to collect Prometheus metrics and container logs without running your own stack. The mapping to this module: Prometheus ~ Azure Monitor metrics, Grafana ~ Metrics Explorer/dashboards (or Grafana with the Azure data source), EFK ~ Log Analytics + KQL, Alertmanager ~ Azure Monitor alert rules with action groups. Worked example: replicate the checkout RED dashboard natively. Solution: Container Insights collects the Prometheus endpoints; a Log Analytics query (KQL) aggregates: ContainerLog | where LogEntry contains 'ERROR' | summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m); an alert rule fires an action group (email + webhook + PagerDuty) when the 5xx ratio crosses the SLO threshold. The decision framework: run Prometheus/Grafana/EFK yourself for portability and PromQL familiarity across clouds (the multicloud answer from M44), or adopt Azure Monitor for zero-operational-overhead on Azure with KQL as the query skill. Most enterprises end up hybrid: Prometheus for K8s metrics, Azure Monitor for platform/audit logs.

notes.title: Observability at Millions of Transactions per Second
notes.body: The panel asks how you do logging and monitoring at millions of transactions per second — the answer is sampling, aggregation, and cardinality discipline, because naive 'log everything, label everything' collapses. Metrics: keep label cardinality bounded — a label with a million distinct values (like user_id or request_id) creates a million time series and will OOM your Prometheus; aggregate at the edge and drop high-cardinality labels via relabeling. Use recording rules to precompute expensive queries (the 5xx ratio per service computed once, read by every dashboard). Logs: sample aggressively (1% of success logs, 100% of errors), structure everything, and ship to a tiered store. Traces: head-based sampling at low rates plus tail-based sampling that keeps all error traces — you need the failures, not the successes. Worked example: checkout does 2M txns/sec; the team wants per-request logs and per-user latency metrics. Solution: per-user latency as a metric is rejected (cardinality explosion); instead histogram by route with bounded labels, recording rules for the SLO ratios, 1% sampled success logs + 100% error logs, and tail-sampled traces keeping errors. The panel one-liner: 'At scale, observability is a sampling and aggregation architecture, not a collection architecture.'

quiz.q: Which PromQL query gives per-service requests per second?
quiz.explain: rate() converts the counter to per-second; sum by (service) aggregates across instances. Bare counters and avg() are meaningless for rates.

quiz.q: You need p99 checkout latency. Which is correct?
quiz.explain: Quantiles come from histogram buckets via histogram_quantile; avg/max of raw observations are not available from aggregated exposition and max is not p99.

quiz.q: A dashboard panel shows rate(queue_depth[5m]). What is wrong?
choices: queue_depth is a Gauge — rate() on a gauge is meaningless; read it directly
quiz.explain: rate() assumes a cumulative counter and corrects for resets; applied to a gauge it fabricates values. Gauges are read as-is or smoothed with avg_over_time.

quiz.q: Checkout errors spike. Fastest EFK triage path?
choices: Kibana: filter level=error AND service=checkout over the window, aggregate by error_code, pivot on trace_id
Increase log verbosity to debug everywhere

quiz.q: At 2M txns/sec, the team wants a per-user-id latency metric. Your response?
choices: Reject: cardinality explosion — a million label values means a million time series; use bounded labels + histograms + recording rules

quiz.q: Which sampling strategy keeps all error traces at high throughput?

quiz.explain: Tail-based sampling decides after seeing the outcome, so it can keep 100% of failures while dropping the bulk of successes.

quiz.q: A recording rule precomputes the per-service 5xx ratio. Why?
choices: Expensive queries run once at scrape time instead of on every dashboard load and alert evaluation
quiz.explain: Recording rules trade a little storage for a lot of query-time savings — critical when many dashboards and alerts share the same ratio.

quiz.q: Debug logging is enabled in production at high throughput and the logging bill explodes. What are the two fixes?
choices: Per-environment log levels (info in prod) plus sampling of high-volume success logs, with tiered retention
quiz.explain: Volume control happens at the source (levels, sampling) and at the store (hot/warm/delete retention tiers). Scaling the store without fixing the source just moves the bill.
