title: Alerting, SLOs & Incident Response
summary: Run reliability as an engineering discipline: SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets with real math, burn-rate alerting, on-call routing, incident command, blameless postmortems, and runbooks you prove in a live drill.
objectives: Define SLIs/SLOs and compute error budgets, applying freeze policies to ship-vs-stabilize decisions
Configure fast-burn and slow-burn alerts and explain why burn rate beats absolute thresholds
Design alert routing chains and on-call escalation with alert-quality rules
Run incidents with roles and the mitigate-first protocol, then write blameless postmortems with Five Whys
Write, execute, and maintain runbooks proven in live drills

notes.title: SLIs, SLOs, and Error Budgets
notes.body: A Service Level Indicator (SLI) is what you measure — e.g. the fraction of checkout requests that succeed within 500ms. A Service Level Objective (SLO) is the target — 99.9% of checkouts succeed within 500ms over a 30-day window. The error budget is the allowed failure: 100% minus the SLO, so 99.9% leaves a 0.1% budget. Error budgets turn reliability into a currency: while budget remains, the team may ship features and take risks; when the budget burns out, all engineering effort shifts to reliability until it recovers. Worked example: checkout serves 10 million requests in 30 days with a 99.9% SLO. Error budget = 0.1% x 10M = 10,000 failed requests. After a bad deploy causes 8,000 failures in one day, the remaining budget is 2,000 — the release freeze policy triggers (say, below 25% remaining), so the next two feature releases are held and the team works on the flaky payment dependency instead. Solution logic: budgets make the ship-vs-stabilize tradeoff explicit and pre-agreed, so it is policy, not politics. The trap: SLOs without consequences are vanity metrics — an SLO nobody acts on teaches the organization to ignore all SLOs.

notes.title: Burn Rate: How Fast Are You Spending Reliability?
notes.body: Burn rate measures how fast the error budget is being consumed relative to the SLO window. A burn rate of 1 spends budget exactly on target; 10 burns ten times too fast. Alerting on burn rate (rather than raw error counts) is the Google SRE practice because it is self-normalizing: it works for 10 requests/sec and 10,000 alike. The standard setup uses two alert speeds: a fast-burn alert (e.g. burn rate 14 over 1 hour — pages immediately, you will exhaust budget in days) and a slow-burn alert (burn rate 3 over 6 hours — tickets, you are leaking budget steadily). Worked example: SLO 99.9% over 30 days; in the last hour, errors ran at 2% against a 0.1% budget. Burn rate = 2% / 0.1% = 20. At this pace the 30-day budget dies in 1.5 days — page now. Contrast: errors at 0.3% sustained for 6 hours gives burn rate 3 — a ticket, investigated today, not a 3 AM page. Solution: configure both alerts; the fast one protects the budget, the slow one catches the bleed. The anti-pattern is alerting on absolute thresholds ('more than 100 errors') — it pages the low-traffic service for noise and sleeps through the high-traffic service's real outage. Burn rate alerts scale with the service.

notes.title: Alert Routing and On-Call Design
notes.body: Alerts must reach the right human with the right context in minutes. The routing chain: detection (Prometheus alert rule or Azure Monitor alert) -> notification grouping (Alertmanager groups by service/severity to prevent 200 separate pages for one outage) -> on-call schedule (who is primary this week) -> escalation policy (no ack in 10 min -> secondary; 20 min -> manager). Alert quality rules: every page must be actionable (the runbook link tells you what to do), every page must be urgent (if it can wait until morning, it is a ticket, not a page), and alerts need severity tiers — critical (page), warning (ticket), info (dashboard). Worked example: design routing for the checkout service. Solution: Prometheus rule 'CheckoutHighErrorBudgetBurn' (fast-burn) -> Alertmanager route matching service=checkout, severity=critical -> PagerDuty/on-call primary with a runbook link to the checkout triage doc; slow-burn -> ticketing queue with a 4-hour SLA; deploy annotations feed the dashboard so the responder sees what shipped. The on-call health metric: pages per shift. More than 2-3 pages per on-call week means the alerts are miscalibrated or the service is genuinely unhealthy — either way, the fix is engineering, not heroics. Alert fatigue kills response quality faster than any outage.

notes.title: Incident Roles and the First 30 Minutes
notes.body: Incidents need roles, not heroes. The three core roles: Incident Commander (coordinates, makes decisions, keeps the timeline — does NOT debug), Communications Lead (status page and stakeholder updates every 15-30 minutes), and Responders (diagnose and mitigate). The first-30-minutes protocol: (1) declare the incident and page the roles (2 min); (2) assess blast radius from dashboards — which services, which users, since when (5 min); (3) mitigate first, root-cause later — roll back the deploy, fail over, shed load, or flip the feature flag (10 min); (4) communicate the current status and next update time (ongoing). Worked example: checkout p99 triples at 14:02, deploy went out at 13:55. The Responder wants to read code; the Commander orders the rollback first. Solution: rollback at 14:08, p99 recovers by 14:12, incident downgraded — root-causing the bad query happens after, in the postmortem, with no users still bleeding. The principle: mitigation before diagnosis. Every minute of 'let me just check one thing' while users fail is a choice to keep the outage running. Declare early — a false alarm costs a page; a late declaration costs an outage.

notes.title: Blameless Postmortems and the Five Whys
notes.body: A blameless postmortem asks what allowed the failure, never who caused it — because blame suppresses the reporting that prevention depends on. The document has a fixed shape: summary, impact (duration, affected users/requests), timeline (detection, mitigation, resolution with timestamps), root causes (usually 2-3 contributing factors, never one), and action items (each with an owner and a due date — an action item without an owner is a wish). The Five Whys drill past the proximate cause: 'Checkout failed' -> why? 'Payment service timed out' -> why? 'Its connection pool was exhausted' -> why? 'A retry storm from the bad deploy multiplied load 8x' -> why? 'No retry budget or circuit breaker on that client' -> why? 'Resilience patterns were never added to the integration checklist.' The fix lands at the fifth why, not the first. Worked example: write the action items for the retry-storm outage. Solution: (1) add circuit breaker + retry budgets to the payment client — owner: payments team, due in 2 weeks; (2) add a deploy-canary error-budget gate — owner: platform team, due in 1 month; (3) load-test retry behavior in staging — owner: QA, due in 3 weeks. Each is verifiable; each prevents recurrence rather than punishing the deployer.

notes.title: Runbooks: The Lab You Write Before the Fire
notes.body: A runbook is the written procedure for a known failure mode — diagnosis steps, mitigation commands, escalation criteria, and rollback instructions — kept where the on-call can reach it at 3 AM. A good runbook has: symptoms (what the alert looks like), blast radius check (the two dashboard links), diagnosis (the exact kubectl/PromQL/KQL commands), mitigation (the exact commands, copy-pasteable), escalation (when to wake the secondary, when to declare a major incident), and rollback. Runbooks decay: every postmortem must update the runbook it used, and runbooks get a quarterly review owner. Worked example: the checkout error-budget runbook. Symptoms: fast-burn alert fires. Diagnosis: (1) kubectl get pods -n checkout (CrashLoopBackOff?); (2) Prometheus: 5xx ratio by pod (one pod or all?); (3) check deploy annotations (did something just ship?). Mitigation: if one bad pod — kubectl delete pod to reschedule; if post-deploy — kubectl rollout undo deployment/checkout; if downstream — flip the payment feature flag off. Escalation: no improvement in 15 min -> page secondary + declare major. Solution review: every step is a command, not prose; the responder never has to invent triage while stressed. The lab below has you write and then execute one — because a runbook you have never run is a rumor, not a procedure.

Fast-burn error-budget alert with a runbook link and a mitigation command
quiz.explain: Pages must be actionable and urgent. Disk at 70% is a ticket; the burn alert names the failure and the fix.

quiz.q: During an incident, the Responder wants to keep debugging while users fail. The Commander should:
choices: Order mitigation first (rollback/failover) — diagnosis happens after users stop bleeding
quiz.explain: Mitigation before diagnosis is the core protocol; root-causing belongs in the postmortem, not in the outage window.

quiz.q: Who writes the status updates during an incident?
quiz.explain: Dedicated comms role on a cadence keeps stakeholders informed and keeps responders free to mitigate.

quiz.q: A postmortem action item reads 'be more careful next time'. What is wrong?
choices: No owner, no due date, not verifiable — it is blame in disguise, not prevention
quiz.explain: Action items need owner + due date + verifiability, and must fix the system (the fifth why), not scold the human.

quiz.q: Five Whys on a retry-storm outage ends at 'resilience patterns were never in the integration checklist'. What does this tell you?
choices: The systemic fix: add circuit breakers/retry budgets to the checklist — the first why (timeout) was only the proximate cause
quiz.explain: The fifth why reveals the process gap; fixing it prevents the whole class of outage. Stopping at the first why just restarts the timer.

quiz.q: On-call gets 8 pages a week, all actionable but exhausting. What is the correct response?
choices: Treat it as an engineering problem: recalibrate thresholds, fix flaky alerts, and address the underlying reliability debt
quiz.explain: Pages-per-shift is a health metric; sustained high paging means miscalibrated alerts or real unreliability — both fixed with engineering, not endurance.

drills.title: Timed drill: SLO math under pressure

items.prompt: Define SLI, SLO, error budget in one breath.
items.answer: SLI: what you measure. SLO: the target over a window. Budget: 100% minus SLO — the allowed failures.
items.explain: One breath, three terms — the panel's warm-up.

items.prompt: 10M requests, 99.9% SLO. Budget?
items.answer: 10,000 failed requests per 30 days.
items.explain: 0.1% of 10M — show the arithmetic, not just the number.

items.prompt: 8,000 failures spent, freeze policy at 25% remaining. Decision?
items.answer: 20% remains — below threshold: freeze features, shift to reliability.
items.explain: Policy makes it automatic — say 'pre-agreed, not political'.

items.prompt: Errors at 2%/hour vs 0.1% budget. Burn rate and action?
items.answer: Burn rate 20 — page now; budget dies in ~1.5 days.
items.explain: Observed/budget = 20. Fast-burn = page.

items.prompt: Errors at 0.3% for 6 hours. Burn rate and action?
items.answer: Burn rate 3 — ticket for today; slow-burn leak.
items.explain: Contrast with the previous item — the panel wants both speeds.

items.prompt: Why burn-rate alerts instead of 'more than 100 errors'?
items.answer: Self-normalizing: absolute counts page quiet services for noise and miss loud-service outages.
items.explain: Scales with the service — the SRE-correct answer.

items.prompt: SLO with no consequences is what?
items.answer: A vanity metric — teaches the org to ignore all SLOs.
items.explain: Consequences (freeze policy) are what make SLOs real.

items.prompt: Name the three incident roles and the Commander's one rule.
items.answer: Commander (coordinates, never debugs), Comms Lead (updates every 15-30 min), Responders (mitigate).
items.explain: The Commander's rule — does not debug — is what the panel listens for.

items.prompt: First 30 minutes: the four beats.
items.answer: Declare+page, assess blast radius, mitigate first, communicate on cadence.
items.explain: Say the timeboxes: 2 / 5 / 10 minutes, then ongoing comms.

items.prompt: p99 triples 7 minutes after a deploy. First action?
items.answer: Rollback the deploy — mitigation before diagnosis.
items.explain: Users are bleeding; root-cause later in the postmortem.

items.prompt: Postmortem fixed shape — the five sections.
items.answer: Summary, impact, timeline, root causes, action items (owner + due date).
items.explain: Recite all five; stress owner+date on actions.

items.prompt: Run the Five Whys on: 'checkout failed because payment timed out.'
items.answer: Timeout -> pool exhausted -> retry storm 8x load -> no retry budget/circuit breaker -> never in the integration checklist.
items.explain: End at the systemic gap — that is where the fix lives.

items.prompt: Write one good action item for the retry storm.
items.answer: 'Add circuit breaker + retry budgets to payment client — owner: payments team, due in 2 weeks.'
items.explain: Verifiable, owned, dated, systemic — the four tests.

items.prompt: A runbook section list — name all six.
items.answer: Symptoms, blast-radius check, diagnosis commands, mitigation commands, escalation criteria, rollback.
items.explain: Copy-pasteable commands, not prose — runnable at 3 AM.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: burn-rate alerts, on-call routing, and a live incident drill
handsOnLab.brief: You will define SLIs/SLOs for a sample service, build fast-burn and slow-burn alerts, design the on-call routing chain, write a runbook, and then run a simulated incident against it — including the postmortem.

Write the Prometheus alert rules: fast-burn (burn rate 14, 1h window, severity critical) and slow-burn (burn rate 3, 6h window, severity warning) for the success-ratio SLI.

Hold the postmortem: write summary, impact, timeline with timestamps, root causes via Five Whys, and 3 action items with owners and due dates.
Update the runbook with everything the drill exposed; set a quarterly review reminder and owner.
Compute your drill metrics: time-to-detect, time-to-mitigate, pages received; compare against your SLO policy targets.
Write the on-call improvement note: given your drill paging volume, are the thresholds right? What would you retune?

title: Shift-Left Security: SAST/DAST & Dependency Scanning
summary: Push security into the developer workflow: SAST/DAST/IAST lenses, dependency scanning, pipeline gates with real teeth, Trivy image scanning in CI, governed triage, and the OWASP coverage map panels expect.
objectives: Distinguish SAST, DAST, and IAST and place each correctly in the pipeline
Scan dependencies with npm audit, pip-audit, and related SCA tooling
Design pipeline security gates with thresholds and speed-appropriate placement
Scan container images with Trivy in CI and remediate via the base-first ladder
Run governed triage with allowlists, metrics, and an OWASP coverage map

notes.title: SAST, DAST, and IAST: Three Different Lenses
notes.body: Shift-left means finding vulnerabilities where they are cheapest to fix — in the developer's workflow, not in production. Three techniques cover three lenses. SAST (Static Application Security Testing) reads source code without running it: it finds SQL injection patterns, hardcoded secrets, and insecure crypto before the code ever executes. Tools: Semgrep (semgrep scan --config auto), Bandit for Python (bandit -r src/), CodeQL. DAST (Dynamic AST) attacks the running application: OWASP ZAP spiders the site and fires payloads at it, finding what static analysis cannot — authentication flaws, server misconfigurations, runtime injection. IAST (Interactive AST) instruments the running app (an agent inside the JVM/CLR) and watches real execution, combining code context with runtime proof. Worked example: where does each catch a SQL injection? SAST flags the string-concatenated query at commit time; DAST proves it by injecting ' OR '1'='1 into the live login form in staging; IAST watches the test suite execute the vulnerable path and reports the exact tainted-data flow. The panel point: SAST is fast and early but noisy; DAST is proof but late and needs a running environment; IAST is precise but requires instrumentation. Mature pipelines run SAST on every PR, DAST nightly against staging, IAST in integration tests.

notes.title: Dependency (SCA) Scanning: Your Code Is 10% Yours
notes.body: Modern applications are overwhelmingly third-party code — frameworks, transitive dependencies, native packages — and vulnerabilities arrive through them (the supply-chain reality behind every 'critical CVE in a library you never chose'). SCA (Software Composition Analysis) scans your dependency manifests and lockfiles against vulnerability databases. The commands are built into your toolchain: npm audit (and npm audit fix, carefully), pip-audit -r requirements.txt for Python, dotnet list package --vulnerable, cargo audit, go list with govulncheck. The pipeline step fails the build on critical/high CVEs, with an allowlist for accepted risks that carries an expiry date and an owner — never a permanent ignore. Worked example: pip-audit reports CVE-2024-XXXX critical in requests 2.28.0 via requirements.txt. Solution: (1) confirm exploitability — is the vulnerable code path reachable? (2) upgrade to the patched 2.32.x and run the test suite; (3) if the upgrade breaks, evaluate the backported patch or isolate the call path, and only then add a time-boxed exception with owner and review date. The trap: npm audit fix blindly upgrading majors and breaking the build the night before release — pin versions (the M50 requirements.txt lesson), review the diff, and let CI prove the upgrade.

notes.title: Pipeline Security Gates: Fail the Build, Not the Audit
notes.body: A security gate is a pipeline stage that blocks promotion when risk exceeds policy: SAST findings above threshold, critical CVEs in dependencies, container image vulnerabilities, or leaked secrets. Gate design matters more than gate existence. Thresholds: fail on critical always; fail on high unless allowlisted with expiry; warn on medium. Placement: fast checks (SAST, SCA, secret scan) on every pull request where the developer can fix in minutes; slow checks (full DAST, image scan of the final artifact) on merge to main before staging deploy. Worked example: a Jenkins/GitHub Actions stage after unit tests: run trivy on the built image, semgrep on the diff, pip-audit on requirements. If any critical appears, the stage fails, the PR is blocked, and the finding links to the exact line and the fix guidance. Solution review: the developer fixes it in the PR in ten minutes; the alternative — found in a quarterly audit — costs a ticket, a meeting, and a hotfix. The anti-pattern is the advisory-only gate that everyone ignores: a gate that never blocks is a dashboard, not a control. Start strict on new code (block), advisory on legacy (ratchet), and tighten the ratchet quarterly.

notes.title: Container Image Scanning in CI with Trivy
notes.body: Container images bundle an OS userland plus your app, so they inherit every CVE in both. Scanning the final image in CI — after build, before push — is the choke point: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:pr-123 fails the pipeline on high/critical findings. Scan the base image separately and regularly, because base CVEs arrive without any code change on your part. The remediation ladder: (1) rebuild on a patched base (use minimal bases — distroless or alpine — to shrink the CVE surface); (2) update the application dependencies; (3) only then, allowlist a specific CVE with expiry when it is provably unreachable. Worked example: trivy flags CRITICAL CVE-2024-YYYY in openssl inside your python:3.11 base. Solution: check for python:3.11-slim patched tag or the distroless variant, rebuild, rescan — the finding should clear; if the patch is not yet released, document the exposure window, add a 14-day allowlist with owner, and set a calendar reminder, not a permanent ignore. The M-series callback: this is the Dockerfile lesson made operational — multi-stage builds and minimal bases from the Docker module are what make these scans passable in the first place.

notes.title: Triaging Findings: Signal, Noise, and the Allowlist
notes.body: Scanners produce findings; engineers produce judgments. Triage sorts every finding into: true positive and exploitable (fix now), true positive but unreachable (allowlist with expiry and justification), false positive (suppress with reason, revisit on tool upgrade), and duplicate (dedupe to the root cause). The allowlist is a governed document, not a junk drawer: each entry has the CVE/finding ID, why it is accepted (unreachable path, compensating control), an owner, and an expiry date — expired entries re-alert automatically. Metrics keep the program honest: mean time to remediate criticals, percentage of findings allowlisted (a rising share means the gate is being bypassed culturally), and scanner coverage (what percentage of repos run the gates). Worked example: SAST flags 'hardcoded password' on test fixtures using 'password123' against a local test database. Solution: true positive pattern, unreachable in production — but the right fix is not an allowlist, it is moving the fixture to a secrets-free test helper; allowlist only when the code cannot be made clean. The panel point: 'How do you handle false positives?' is a culture question — the answer is a governed triage process with expiry, not 'we ignore the scanner.'

notes.title: Mapping to OWASP: What the Scanners Are Hunting
notes.body: The OWASP Top 10 is the shared vocabulary for what all this tooling hunts: injection (SAST + DAST), broken access control (DAST + manual review), cryptographic failures (SAST flags weak algorithms), vulnerable components (SCA), security misconfiguration (DAST + image scan), and the rest. Each pipeline gate maps to categories: SAST covers injection and crypto; SCA covers vulnerable components; DAST covers access control, misconfiguration, and auth failures; image scanning covers the platform layer beneath the app. Worked example: map a pipeline to the Top 10 for a panel. Solution: 'PR gates — Semgrep (injection, crypto), pip-audit/npm audit (vulnerable components), gitleaks (secrets, feeding M48); merge gates — Trivy image scan (misconfiguration, known OS CVEs); nightly — ZAP baseline against staging (access control, auth, misconfiguration). Every Top 10 category has at least one automated check, and the allowlist governs the exceptions.' The interview move: never recite the Top 10 as trivia — narrate it as your pipeline's coverage map. That turns a memorization question into an architecture answer, which is exactly what senior panels reward.

quiz.q: Where does SAST catch a SQL injection, and where does DAST prove it?
choices: SAST at commit time flags the concatenated query; DAST proves it by injecting into the live staging login form
quiz.explain: SAST sees the code pattern early; DAST demonstrates exploitability against the running app. IAST would trace the tainted flow during tests.

quiz.q: pip-audit reports a critical CVE in requests 2.28.0. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Confirm exploitability -> upgrade to patched version and run tests -> time-boxed exception only if upgrade is impossible

quiz.q: Which gate placement is correct?
choices: Fast checks (SAST/SCA/secret scan) per PR; slow checks (full DAST, final image scan) on merge
All security testing once a year
quiz.explain: Speed-appropriate placement: PR gates give ten-minute fixes; merge gates protect staging; nightly DAST covers depth.

choices: The image contains HIGH or CRITICAL findings, so the pipeline stage fails and the PR is blocked

choices: Fix the code: move fixtures to a secrets-free helper; allowlist only what cannot be made clean

title: Secrets, Supply Chain & Identity
summary: Lock down the last mile: Vault/Key Vault secret management with practiced rotation, the secrets-in-git ritual, SBOMs and cosign signing, least-privilege RBAC across five layers, and the Security+ domain crosswalk.
objectives: Manage secrets in Vault/Key Vault with dynamic credentials and rehearsed rotation
Prevent, detect, and remediate secrets committed to git with gitleaks gates
Generate SBOMs and sign container images, enforcing verification at deploy time
Apply least-privilege RBAC across Kubernetes, cloud, application, database, and pipeline layers
Map secrets and supply-chain work to CompTIA Security+ domains for panel conversations

notes.title: Secret Management: Vault and Key Vault
notes.body: Secrets — API keys, database passwords, TLS private keys — must live in a purpose-built secret store, never in code, config files, or chat. HashiCorp Vault and Azure Key Vault provide the same core contract: encrypted storage, fine-grained access policies, audit logging of every read, dynamic secrets (credentials generated on demand with a TTL, e.g. a database password that lives 1 hour), and rotation. The access pattern: the application authenticates to Vault (via Kubernetes auth, Azure auth, or AppRole — never a hardcoded token in production) and reads the secret at startup or via a sidecar injector; CI pipelines fetch secrets at runtime from the store instead of storing them as pipeline variables. Worked example: a Flask app needs the Postgres password. Anti-pattern: DATABASE_URL with the password in the deployment YAML committed to git. Solution: store it with vault kv put secret/checkout db_password=<value>; the pod uses the Vault agent injector annotation to render the secret into a file at startup; rotation is vault kv put with the new value plus a database password change — no redeploy, no git history. On Azure the equivalent is az keyvault secret set --vault-name kv-prod --name db-password, referenced from AKS via the Secrets Store CSI driver. The audit property is the point: the store logs who read what, when — something env vars and files can never do.

notes.title: Rotation and the Blast Radius of a Leak
notes.body: Every secret has a lifetime, and rotation is how you bound the blast radius when (not if) one leaks. Static secrets should rotate on a schedule (90 days is the common policy; 30 for high-value) and immediately on any suspected exposure, personnel departure, or the 'it was in a Slack thread' incident. Dynamic secrets are better: Vault generates a database credential per application instance with a 1-hour TTL — there is nothing long-lived to leak, and revocation is automatic. The rotation procedure must be rehearsed: (1) generate the new secret in the store; (2) update consumers (rolling restart or sidecar re-render); (3) verify the new credential works; (4) revoke the old one; (5) confirm nothing still uses it via the audit log. Worked example: an AWS access key was pasted into a public Slack channel. Solution sequence: immediately deactivate (not delete — preserve for forensics) the key in IAM, generate a replacement, update the one consumer via the secret store, verify, then delete the old key; search git history and logs for the key string; write the postmortem on how a long-lived key ended up copy-pasteable. The lesson the panel wants: the incident is survivable because rotation was a practiced procedure, not an improvisation — and the long-term fix is replacing the key with an OIDC-assumed role so there is no key to leak next time.

notes.title: Secrets in Git: The Antipattern and Its Detection
notes.body: Committing a secret to git publishes it to every clone, fork, and backup forever — deleting it later does not unpublish it, because history retains it. Prevention is a pipeline gate: gitleaks detect --no-git (or the pre-commit hook gitleaks protect) scans diffs for key patterns and fails the PR before the secret lands. Detection on existing repos: gitleaks detect --source . --verbose across history finds what is already burned. Remediation of a burned secret is a fixed ritual: (1) revoke/rotate the secret immediately — it is compromised, full stop; (2) purge it from history only if the repo can tolerate a force-push (git filter-repo), understanding clones still have it; (3) audit where the secret was valid during exposure (cloud audit logs); (4) add the gitleaks gate so it cannot recur. Worked example: gitleaks flags AKIA... in a commit from 6 months ago. Solution: the key is burned — rotate it now, check CloudTrail for usage of that key ID during the window, purge history if the team accepts the force-push, and enable the pre-commit hook today. The interview answer: 'A secret in git is a compromised secret; rotation first, history surgery second, prevention gate third.' Never 'we deleted the file so it is fine.'

notes.title: Supply Chain: SBOMs and Signing
notes.body: You cannot secure what you cannot inventory: an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) lists every component in your artifact — OS packages, language dependencies, base image layers. Generate it in CI: syft packages myapp:tag -o spdx-json > sbom.json produces a machine-readable inventory you attach to the release. Signing proves the artifact you deploy is the artifact you built: cosign sign --key cosign.key myapp:tag (or keyless with OIDC via cosign sign --oidc-issuer) creates a signature; admission controllers verify it before pods start — unsigned images do not run. The chain: SBOM generation -> vulnerability scan of the SBOM -> sign the artifact -> verify at deploy time. Worked example: a critical CVE is announced in a base-image library at 9 AM. With SBOMs: query which of your 40 services' SBOMs contain the library version — 3 do; rebuild and resign those 3 by noon. Without SBOMs: manually audit 40 Dockerfiles and guess. Solution review: the SBOM turns a fire drill into a database query, and signing guarantees the rebuilt images are the ones that deploy. The panel framing: SBOM answers 'what is in it?', signing answers 'did we build it?', and together they are the supply-chain answer to 'how do you know what is running in prod?'

notes.title: RBAC and Least Privilege Across the Full Stack
notes.body: The panel asks about RBAC across a full-stack app — the answer spans every layer with one principle: least privilege, each identity getting only what its job requires. Kubernetes RBAC: Roles/ClusterRoles bound to ServiceAccounts via RoleBindings — the checkout ServiceAccount gets get/list on its own ConfigMaps, not cluster-admin. Cloud IAM: the patterns from M42/M43 (IRSA, Workload Identity) scoped to single buckets/queues. Application layer: role checks in the API (admin vs analyst vs viewer), row-level filtering on queries, and the database user granted SELECT on exactly the tables it needs. Pipeline: the deploy identity can apply to the staging namespace but needs an approval gate for prod. Worked example: design access for a data analyst who needs read-only dashboards. Solution: cloud IAM read-only role on the warehouse; Kubernetes read-only ClusterRole on the analytics namespace; application role 'viewer' with no export permission; database GRANT SELECT on the marts schema only; no CI deploy rights; no secret-store read. Every layer says the minimum. The failure mode is role explosion (400 custom roles nobody understands) — counter it with a small set of standard roles per layer, reviewed quarterly, with every exception carrying an owner and expiry, exactly like the M47 allowlist discipline.

notes.title: CompTIA Security+ Domain Crosswalk
notes.body: This module maps cleanly onto the CompTIA Security+ domains, which is useful interview framing: the domains are the industry's shared checklist, and narrating your work against them shows structured thinking. Domain 1 (General Security Concepts): least privilege, zero trust, and the control types your gates implement. Domain 2 (Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations): CVE triage, supply-chain attacks, and secret exposure as threat vectors. Domain 3 (Security Architecture): secret stores, signing infrastructure, and network segmentation for secret access. Domain 4 (Security Operations): rotation procedures, incident handling for leaks, log auditing of secret access, and vulnerability scanning operations. Domain 5 (Security Program Management): the allowlist governance, rotation policies, and compliance evidence (who accessed what secret when) that auditors ask for. Worked example: a panel asks 'how does your secrets program map to Security+?' Solution: 'Architecture gives us Vault/Key Vault with dynamic secrets; Operations gives us rotation runbooks and leak incident procedures with audit logs; Program Management gives us the 90-day rotation policy and the governed exception process — and the scanners from M47 feed the vulnerability management in Domain 4.' The point is not the certification — this course confers none — it is speaking the domain language that security-minded panels expect.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: Vault, gitleaks gates, SBOMs, and signed images
handsOnLab.brief: You will run Vault in dev mode, wire secret injection into a sample app, plant and catch a git secret with gitleaks, generate SBOMs, sign an image with cosign, and verify the signature — the full supply-chain loop.
steps: Start Vault dev server: vault server -dev (dev only); export VAULT_ADDR and VAULT_TOKEN; enable KV v2 at secret/.
Store the app secret: vault kv put secret/labapp db_password='s3cret-lab-only'; create a policy allowing read on secret/labapp/*.
Deploy the sample app with the Vault agent injector annotation; exec into the pod and confirm the secret renders as a file with no secret in env or git.
Rotate: vault kv put a new value; restart the deployment; confirm the app picks it up with zero code changes.
Plant a fake AWS key in a commit; run gitleaks detect --source . --verbose; record the finding with commit SHA.
Execute the burned-secret ritual on paper: rotate (simulate), list what you would audit, and decide on history purge with justification.
Add the gitleaks pre-commit hook; attempt to commit another fake key and confirm the commit is blocked.
Build the app image; generate the SBOM: syft packages labapp:1.0 -o spdx-json > sbom.json; record the OS + language package counts.
Run trivy against the SBOM/image; for one finding, write the allowlist entry (ID, justification, owner, 14-day expiry).
Generate a cosign key pair; sign: cosign sign --key cosign.key labapp:1.0; verify: cosign verify --key cosign.pub labapp:1.0.

Simulate admission: write the policy snippet (e.g. Kyverno/Gatekeeper pseudo-policy) requiring valid cosign signatures on the lab namespace; confirm an unsigned tag would be rejected by your rule logic.
Write the Security+ crosswalk paragraph for your lab: which domain each piece belongs to. Tear down Vault and the images.

title: SRE & Resilience: HA, Microservices & the Strangler Fig
summary: Engineer reliability: SRE principles, layered high availability, timeout/retry/circuit-breaker arithmetic, the strangler-fig migration of a monolithic trading platform, chaos game-days, and Little's Law capacity planning.
objectives: Apply SRE principles: error budgets, toil reduction, golden signals, blameless postmortems
Design multi-AZ and multi-region architectures with honest availability math
Implement timeouts, bounded retries, and circuit breakers, computing retry amplification
Plan a strangler-fig migration seam by seam with data migration and fallback safety
Run chaos experiments and capacity-plan with Little's Law

notes.title: SRE Principles: Toil, Budgets, and Blamelessness
notes.body: Site Reliability Engineering treats operations as a software problem. Its principles, straight from the Google SRE tradition: (1) error budgets (M46) govern the feature-vs-reliability tradeoff; (2) toil — manual, repetitive operational work — is budgeted and automated away, with a standing cap on how much of a team's time it may consume; (3) monitoring is built around the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation); (4) automation is preferred over heroics for every repeated task; (5) blameless postmortems turn incidents into system fixes. The SRE mindset shift for a panel: reliability is a feature with a price, negotiated explicitly via the SLO — not a vague aspiration. Worked example: a team spends 60% of its time on manual deploy verifications and ticket-driven restarts. SRE analysis: that is toil — automatable, repetitive, and scaling linearly with service count. Solution: cap toil work, automate the deploy verification into the pipeline (smoke tests + automatic rollback on burn-rate alerts), and convert the restart tickets into the autoscaler + health-probe fixes from M41. The interview one-liner: 'SRE replaces operational heroics with engineering: budgets decide priorities, automation absorbs toil, and postmortems fix systems.'

notes.title: High Availability: Multi-AZ and Multi-Region Design
notes.body: High availability is designed in layers. Within a region: deploy across at least 3 availability zones — AKS node pools spread with --zones 1 2 3, databases with zone-redundant replicas, load balancers zone-aware. A zone failure then costs capacity, not availability. Across regions: active-passive (traffic on one region, tested failover to the second) for most financial workloads, active-active only when the data layer supports conflict-free replication. The data layer decides everything: stateless services fail over trivially; databases need replication with a known RPO/RTO, and the failover must be rehearsed — an untested failover is a hope. Worked example: design the checkout service for zone failure. Solution: AKS with 3 zones, pod anti-affinity spreading replicas across zones, PodDisruptionBudgets guaranteeing quorum during drains, Azure SQL zone-redundant, Application Gateway multi-zone; chaos-test by failing one zone in staging quarterly. The panel question on 'fault tolerance for mission-critical financial apps' wants exactly this layered answer: multi-AZ for the common case, multi-region with tested failover for the disaster case, data replication as the binding constraint, and rehearsal as the proof. Availability math is honest: each added nine costs roughly an order of magnitude more engineering — 99.9% is 8.8 hours/year of budget, 99.99% is 53 minutes, and the SLO should match what the business will actually fund.

notes.title: Circuit Breakers, Retries, and Timeouts
notes.body: Distributed systems fail partially, and naive clients turn partial failure into total failure. Three patterns contain it. Timeouts: every outbound call gets a deadline (e.g. 2s) — without one, a hung dependency parks your threads forever. Retries: retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter, but only idempotent operations — retrying a non-idempotent payment charge double-charges. Circuit breakers: after N consecutive failures, the breaker opens and calls fail fast for a cooldown period instead of hammering the dead dependency, then half-opens to probe recovery. The retry-storm math the panel loves: service A calls B with 3 retries; B calls C with 3 retries; one slow C means each user request fans out to 1 + 3 + 9 = up to 13 downstream calls — a 13x amplification that melts C. Worked example: payment calls take 200ms normally; the client has no timeout and 5 retries. Under a payment outage, threads pile up waiting, memory grows, and the checkout service itself OOMs — the M41 OOMKilled drill in distributed form. Solution: 2s timeout, max 2 retries with backoff + jitter on idempotent reads only, circuit breaker opening after 5 consecutive failures with 30s cooldown, and a retry budget (e.g. max 10% of requests may be retries). Resilience is arithmetic: bound every fan-out or the fan-out bounds you.

notes.title: Case Study (Hypothetical): Strangler Fig on a Monolithic Trading Platform
notes.body: Exercise — hypothetical, no claims about any real firm: re-architect a legacy monolithic trading platform into microservices. The strangler fig pattern (Martin Fowler) migrates incrementally: new functionality is built as services around the monolith, traffic is routed to the new services piece by piece, and the monolith shrinks until it can be retired — like the fig that grows around a tree. The migration plan: (1) identify seams — order entry, market data, risk checks, settlement — and carve the first low-risk seam (say, market-data fan-out, read-only); (2) put an anti-corruption layer / facade in front of the monolith so new services never touch its schema directly; (3) route via the gateway progressively (1% -> 10% -> 100%) with the monolith as instant fallback; (4) extract state carefully — the database is the hard part, migrated with dual-write or change-data-capture, never a big-bang cutover; (5) retire the monolith's module only when traffic is zero and the data is migrated. Worked example: which seam first? Solution: the read-only market-data feed — no writes, no transactions, easy rollback; order entry (money movement) goes last, with the most testing. The panel answer: 'Strangler fig, seam by seam, gateway-routed with fallback, data migrated via dual-write — never a rewrite, never a big bang.'

notes.title: Chaos Engineering: Proving Resilience on Purpose
notes.body: Chaos engineering is the disciplined practice of injecting failure to prove resilience before production does it for you. Principles: start with a steady-state hypothesis ('checkout p99 stays under 500ms when one zone fails'), blast radius is minimized (staging first, one zone, business-hours, with an abort button), and every experiment is a game-day with observers and a rollback plan. The experiment ladder: kill a pod (does the ReplicaSet recover in seconds?); kill a node (do pods reschedule across zones?); fail a zone (does multi-AZ hold?); inject latency into a dependency (do timeouts and breakers engage?); expire a certificate (does rotation work?). Worked example: hypothesis — 'losing one of three zones keeps checkout under SLO.' Run it in staging: cordon and drain a zone's nodes, watch the dashboards. If p99 breaches, the postmortem writes the missing anti-affinity or PDB as the action item — the experiment paid for itself. The panel framing: chaos is not recklessness, it is the scientific method applied to reliability — hypothesis, controlled experiment, measured result, system fix. Never run chaos in production without the incident-command structure from M46 on standby; the point is learning, not outages.

notes.title: Capacity Planning with Little's Law
notes.body: Little's Law — L = λW — relates the average number of items in a system (L) to the arrival rate (λ) and the average time each spends in the system (W). It is the back-of-the-envelope capacity tool: it needs no distributional assumptions, just consistent units. Worked example: checkout receives λ = 500 requests/second, each taking W = 0.4 seconds of server time. L = 500 × 0.4 = 200 concurrent requests in flight on average. If each pod handles 50 concurrent requests, you need 200/50 = 4 pods for steady state — then add headroom for bursts and rolling updates (the M41 autoscaler math), say min 6. Second example: a queue grows unboundedly. λ = 1000 msgs/s in, processing W-equivalent throughput 800/s — arrivals exceed service, so no steady state exists and the queue grows forever; the fix is more consumers or load shedding, not a bigger queue. The panel callback: combine with the M41 node math — Little's Law gives concurrent load, pod capacity gives pods needed, and the autoscaler min/max brackets the result. Capacity planning is not guessing: it is λ measured from dashboards, W measured from traces, and L computed — then verified by load test.

quiz.explain: L = 500×0.4 = 200 concurrent; 200/50 = 4 pods steady state. Headroom (min 6) covers bursts and update surge — the M41 autoscaler bracket.

items.prompt: Timeout / retry / circuit breaker — one line each.
items.answer: Timeout: deadline per call. Retry: transient + idempotent only, backoff/jitter. Breaker: fail fast after N failures, half-open probe.
items.explain: Then the arithmetic: bound every fan-out.

items.prompt: Retry-storm math: A->B->C, 3 retries each. Amplification?
items.answer: Up to 13x per user request (1+3+9). Bound with retry budgets.
items.explain: Say the number — panels love the 13x.

items.prompt: Which calls may be retried?
items.answer: Idempotent ones only — never money movement.
items.explain: Retrying a charge double-charges. One sentence.

items.prompt: Multi-AZ vs multi-region: when each?
items.answer: Multi-AZ: common case (capacity, not availability). Multi-region active-passive: disaster case, tested failover.
items.explain: Data replication is the binding constraint — say it.

items.prompt: 99.9% vs 99.99% in hours/year?
items.answer: ~8.8 h vs ~53 min. Each nine ~10x the engineering.
items.explain: SLO must match funded reality — the honest-SLO answer.

items.prompt: Zone-failure design: the five pieces?
items.answer: 3 AZs, anti-affinity, PDBs, zone-redundant DB, rehearsed game-day.
items.explain: Recite as the checklist for 'fault tolerance for financial apps'.

items.prompt: Untested failover is ___?
items.answer: A hope, not a plan — rehearse or it fails when needed.
items.explain: One line, no hedging.

items.prompt: Strangler fig in 30 seconds.
items.answer: New services around the monolith; gateway routes traffic piece by piece with fallback; data via dual-write/CDC; retire at zero traffic.
items.explain: Never a rewrite, never a big bang — the mantra.

items.prompt: Trading platform: first seam and last seam?
items.answer: First: read-only market-data feed. Last: order entry (money movement).
items.explain: Risk ordering: stateless reads first, money last.

items.prompt: What does the anti-corruption layer do?
items.answer: Shields new services from the monolith's schema — no legacy coupling.
items.explain: Facade translates; new domain model stays clean.

items.prompt: How is traffic migrated safely?
items.answer: Gateway-routed percentages (1%->10%->100%) with the monolith as instant fallback.
items.explain: Progressive + reversible — the safety property.

items.prompt: How is the database migrated?
items.answer: Dual-write or change-data-capture — never a big-bang cutover.
items.explain: Data is the hard part; say the two techniques.

items.prompt: Little's Law: λ=500, W=0.4. L and pods at 50/pod?
items.answer: L=200; 4 pods steady state, headroom to ~6.
items.explain: Show the arithmetic — λ×W, then divide.

items.prompt: Queue grows forever: diagnosis and fix?
items.answer: λ > service rate: no steady state. Add consumers or shed load.
items.explain: Bigger queue delays; it never fixes.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: resilience patterns and a strangler-fig plan
handsOnLab.brief: You will implement timeout/retry/circuit-breaker in a sample service, measure retry amplification, run a zone-failure game-day on a local cluster, and write the strangler-fig migration plan for a hypothetical monolith.
steps: Write a Python client calling a flaky test server: add a 2s timeout, max 2 retries with exponential backoff + jitter, idempotency keys on writes.
Measure: with retries at 3 per hop across a 2-hop chain, count downstream calls during a 10s induced slowdown — record the amplification factor.
Add a circuit breaker (simple counter-based implementation): open after 5 consecutive failures, 30s cooldown, half-open probe; verify calls fail fast while open.
Add a retry budget: cap retries at 10% of requests; verify the budget throttles retries under sustained failure.
Deploy two services on a local kind cluster across 3 'zones' (labels); set pod anti-affinity and a PodDisruptionBudget; verify spread with kubectl get pods -o wide.
Drain one zone's nodes (kubectl drain); measure recovery time and error rate; record whether the SLO held.
Write the chaos report: hypothesis, blast radius, measurements, and the action items the experiment produced.
Draft the strangler-fig plan for a hypothetical monolithic trading app: seam list in migration order, facade design, gateway routing stages, dual-write data plan, retirement criteria.
Compute capacity with Little's Law for the lab services: measure λ and W from your test traffic, compute L, and compare with actual pod counts.
Define the SLOs for the lab checkout path (success ratio + p99) and the error-budget policy that would freeze the strangler migration.
Present the 5-minute panel narrative: strangler plan, resilience patterns, and the chaos result.
Clean up the kind cluster and archive the plan + report in the repo.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A client library with timeout/retry/breaker/budget, a zone-failure game-day report, a seam-ordered strangler-fig migration plan, and Little's Law capacity math.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Amplification measured and bounded; zone drain recovers within the SLO; the migration plan orders seams by risk with data via dual-write.

Strangler fig: seam-by-seam extraction starting with read-only services, gateway-routed traffic with monolith fallback, anti-corruption layer, data via dual-write/CDC, retire at zero traffic
Lift-and-shift the monolith to bigger VMs

title: BNY Panel Interview Simulation: Independent Mastery
summary: The capstone: every real panel question becomes a timed drill with full model answers, STAR scaffolds for all behavioral questions, delivery coaching, and a complete 90-minute mock panel script you run solo — cold, with no copilot.
objectives: Answer every Terraform/Ansible, Linux, networking, Git, Python, and Docker panel question cold with model-answer depth
Answer every Kubernetes/AKS, Jenkins, Helm, Azure networking, and CI/CD panel question cold
Deliver STAR-structured behavioral answers (unclear requirements, new technology, mentoring) in under 2 minutes

notes.title: The STAR Method: Structure Every Behavioral Answer
notes.body: Behavioral questions are scored on structure, not just content. STAR: Situation (one sentence of context), Task (what you were asked to do), Action (what YOU did — the longest part, first person, specific verbs), Result (measurable outcome + what you learned). Timebox: 90 seconds to 2 minutes; longer rambles lose the panel. The most common failure is staying in Situation for a minute and compressing Action into ten seconds — invert that ratio. Worked example, full model answer for 'Tell me about a time you translated unclear business requirements into technical deliverables.' Situation: 'Our ops team asked for "better visibility into deployments" with no further detail.' Task: 'I needed to turn that into something shippable.' Action: 'I interviewed three on-call engineers for 20 minutes each, mapped their pain to the four golden signals, and proposed a one-page spec: deploy annotations on every dashboard plus a burn-rate alert per service. I validated the spec with the requester before writing code, then built it in two sprints.' Result: 'Deploy-related incidents dropped from "we didn't know what shipped" to a 5-minute correlation, and the one-page spec format became the team's template for vague requests.' Notice: specific verbs (interviewed, mapped, proposed, validated, built), a number, and a transferable lesson. Practice every behavioral answer in this shape until it is muscle memory — the drills below score you on it.

notes.title: STAR Scaffolds: The Three Behavioral Questions
notes.body: Three behavioral questions appear in the panel list; here are complete STAR scaffolds you adapt to your real experience — never invent employers or events, but do bring real ones. (1) 'Translate unclear business requirements into technical deliverables': use the scaffold above — interview stakeholders, write the one-page spec, validate before building, ship incrementally, measure. Your Action must show the translation mechanism (questions asked, spec written), not just 'I figured it out.' (2) 'Introduce a new technology or methodology that improved team performance': Situation — team hand-editing YAML per environment, slow and error-prone. Task — evaluate and introduce a safer way. Action — 'I built a proof-of-concept of Kustomize overlays on one service, demoed the diff to the team, wrote the migration guide, and paired with each service owner for their first conversion.' Result — 'Deploy misconfigurations fell, onboarding a new service went from a day to an hour, and the pattern spread to all 12 services.' The key verb is 'paired' — adoption, not just invention. (3) 'Mentor or upskill developers': Situation — junior engineers struggling with the on-call rotation. Task — get them confident. Action — 'I ran a weekly 30-minute session: week 1 reading dashboards, week 2 the Pending-pod runbook hands-on, week 3 a simulated incident they commanded while I observed.' Result — 'Two juniors took solo on-call within two months with zero escalations in their first rotations.' Mentoring answers must show a curriculum and an outcome, not 'I helped people.'

notes.title: 'Do You Prefer Coding or Infrastructure?' — The Honest Answer
notes.body: This behavioral question is a trap only if you treat it as one. The panel is checking self-awareness and role fit, not loyalty to a tribe. The strong answer is honest, specific, and tied to the role: 'I like both, but I am strongest and happiest at the boundary — writing code that operates infrastructure. I write Python and Go tooling, but I reach for it to solve operational problems: automation, controllers, pipeline logic. Pure application feature work is fine, but my best days are when code I wrote at 10 AM prevents a 2 AM page.' Then bridge to evidence: 'That is why my recent work is Terraform modules, a Prometheus exporter, and the incident runbooks — code in service of reliability.' What not to say: 'I hate coding' (for a DevSecOps role that is disqualifying), 'I only want to code' (wrong role), or a hedged non-answer ('both are great!'). If you genuinely prefer one side, say so and explain why the role still fits: 'I prefer infrastructure, and I code to automate it — which is exactly what this team's platform work needs.' The mock task below drills this as the panel would ask it, with the STAR-shaped reasoning in the explanation.

notes.title: Delivery Coaching: Sound Like You Know It Cold
notes.body: Content without delivery fails panels. Four rules, practiced aloud, recorded, reviewed. (1) Structure first: open every technical answer with the headline, then the points — 'Three reasons: X, Y, Z' — then stop. Panels score organized answers; rambling signals uncertainty even when the facts are right. (2) Slow down: nerves accelerate speech; deliberately speak at two-thirds speed, pause between points, and let the panel absorb. A two-second pause reads as confidence, not hesitation. (3) Camera and presence: look at the camera, not your notes; sit upright; answer as if you are explaining to a colleague, not reciting. Never read — if you must glance at notes, pause, glance, then re-engage the camera and speak. (4) Cold-answer protocol: no copilot, no docs, no pausing the timer. In the drills below, set a timer (60-90 seconds per item), answer aloud, then check the model answer. Mark every item red/yellow/green: red means you could not start, yellow means partial, green means fluent. Reds become tomorrow's study list; the goal is zero reds before you interview. Record yourself weekly — the cringe is the curriculum.

notes.title: The 90-Minute Mock Panel Script (Part 1: Technical Rounds)
notes.body: Run this solo, timed, aloud, no aids — it is the full panel compressed. Round 1 — Introduction (0:00-0:10): deliver your 60-second 'tell me about yourself' (present role, two proof points, why this role), then 2 minutes on your proudest infrastructure project, STAR-shaped. Round 2 — Terraform/IaC deep (0:10-0:30): Terraform vs Ansible and why not just Ansible; removing resources (destroy vs remove block + apply); the storage-account scenario with per-container access types (for_each list to map); state drift and the import with for_each address escaping; how you ran Terraform previously (GitHub, env vars, no tfvars in git, Jenkins credential injection, Vault, Consul); the testing-to-prod lifecycle. Round 3 — Linux, networking, Docker (0:30-0:45): the df-shows-free-but-full triage (inodes, file descriptors, quotas, /tmp); open ports via ss/lsof; A-to-B port check via telnet/nc; the ping/traceroute/telnet connection triage; UDP vs TCP; image size optimization and the RUN/layer/whiteout questions. Round 4 — Kubernetes/AKS (0:45-1:05): pod troubleshooting (get/describe/logs/exec/events); restart loops and exit codes (137 = OOMKilled); the resource request/limit math (16Gi request vs 2Gi need); Pending pods and the node-provisioning checklist; taints vs tolerations vs labels; liveness vs readiness; the Python GIL readiness story; node pools vs one giant pool; App Gateway vs Load Balancer with the traffic flow.

notes.title: The 90-Minute Mock Panel Script (Part 2: CI/CD, Security, Behavioral, Close)
notes.body: Round 5 — CI/CD, Jenkins, Helm, security (1:05-1:20): pipeline phases commit to release and where code is stopped most (unit tests); Groovy in Jenkinsfiles and shared libraries for standardization; why Helm over plain YAML; SAST/DAST/SCA gates and the Trivy image gate; secrets handling (Vault/Key Vault, never in git); RBAC least privilege across the stack. Round 6 — Architecture and scale (1:20-1:30): strangler fig on the monolithic trading platform; HA for mission-critical financial apps; observability at millions of txns/sec (sampling and aggregation); the multicloud strategy answer. Round 7 — Behavioral (1:30-1:45): the three STAR questions (unclear requirements, new technology, mentoring) plus 'prefer coding or infrastructure' — all timed at 2 minutes each, recorded. Round 8 — Your questions and close (1:45-1:50): ask two genuine questions ('How does the team handle on-call load?' 'What does the Terraform workflow look like here — modules, review, apply?'), then close: 'This is exactly the boundary work I do best — I would love to dig into your hardest reliability problem.' Scoring rubric per answer (1-5): accuracy (facts right), completeness (all parts of multi-part questions), structure (headline-first), delivery (pace, camera, no reading). Total 160; passing bar 120 with no reds on safety-critical items (secrets, RBAC, blast radius). Debrief within 24 hours: rewrite every yellow/red answer in full sentences.

notes.title: The Cold-Answer Protocol: Training Without a Copilot
notes.body: The north star of this course is independent mastery: you answer with no copilot, no docs, no second chances — because the panel offers none. The protocol: (1) Daily timed drills — 8 items, 90 seconds each, aloud, scored red/yellow/green; (2) Weekly full mock — the 90-minute script, recorded; (3) Red-team review — for every red, write the full model answer by hand, then re-drill it cold the next day; handwriting recruits memory that typing does not; (4) Teach-back — explain each concept to a rubber duck or study partner as if they are the panel; if you cannot teach it simply, you do not know it; (5) The question bank never shrinks — every question in the spec list stays in rotation until it is green three sessions running. Worked example of a red-to-green cycle: Monday you blank on the for_each import escaping. Monday night you write terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]' <id> ten times with the quoting explained. Tuesday cold drill: green. The panel does not test what you can look up; it tests what you carry. Carry everything in this module, and the interview becomes a demonstration, not an examination.

cards.front: STAR: the four letters + timebox
cards.back: Situation (1 sentence), Task, Action (longest, first-person verbs), Result (measurable + lesson). 90 seconds to 2 minutes

cards.back: A minute of Situation, ten seconds of Action — invert the ratio; Action is what the panel scores

cards.back: Headline, then 'three reasons: X, Y, Z', then stop — organized answers score even when facts are equal

cards.front: Delivery rules 2-4
cards.back: Slow to 2/3 speed with pauses; camera not notes, never read; cold-answer protocol: timer on, no aids

cards.front: Red/yellow/green scoring meaning
cards.back: Red: could not start. Yellow: partial. Green: fluent. Reds become tomorrow's study list; goal is zero reds

cards.front: Exit code 137 = ?
cards.back: OOMKilled (or SIGKILL) — container exceeded its memory limit; check describe lastState + raise limits or fix the leak

cards.front: Rebase vs merge (one line)
cards.back: Merge preserves history with a merge commit; rebase rewrites a linear history — rebase private branches, merge shared ones

cards.back: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]' <id> — quote the whole address so the shell preserves the brackets

cards.back: Delete the block + apply (destroys it), or the 'removed' block to drop it from state without destroying (then apply)

cards.back: telnet <host> <port> or nc -vz <host> <port> — connection success/failure is the answer

cards.front: Pod Running then suddenly restarts: which probe?
cards.back: Liveness — it restarts containers. Readiness only removes from service. Confirm via describe lastState

cards.back: Templating, values per environment, versioned releases with rollback, dependency charts — plain YAML duplicates per env

cards.front: Where do pipelines stop the most code?
cards.back: Unit tests — the earliest, cheapest gate; everything later is more expensive

quiz.q: A behavioral answer spends 60 seconds on Situation and 10 on Action. What is the fix?
choices: Invert the ratio: one sentence of Situation, the bulk on first-person Action with specific verbs, close with measurable Result
quiz.explain: Panels score Action — what YOU did. Situation sets context in one sentence; the verbs and the outcome carry the answer.

quiz.q: You blank on a question mid-panel. Best recovery?
choices: Pause, structure aloud: 'Let me break that into two parts...' and answer what you know precisely
quiz.explain: A structured partial answer ('here is what I know, here is what I would check') scores far above rambling or freezing — it demonstrates engineering thinking.

quiz.q: Container 'svc-basic' terminated with exit code 137. Cause?
choices: OOMKilled — the container exceeded its memory limit (or received SIGKILL); check describe lastState and memory limits
The node ran out of CPU
quiz.explain: 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL); in Kubernetes it is almost always the OOM killer enforcing the memory limit.

quiz.q: Pod requests memory 1Gi but the app needs 2Gi minimum to start. What happens?
choices: It schedules (requests met) then gets OOMKilled when usage exceeds the limit — requests affect scheduling, limits affect survival
quiz.explain: Requests gate scheduling; limits gate survival. Under-provisioned requests schedule fine and die at runtime — the classic OOMKilled trap.

quiz.q: requirements.txt lists: requests, flask, flask-cors, asyncio, setuptools, pandas, pytest — all unpinned. Approve the MR?
choices: Request changes: pin every version (==), remove asyncio (stdlib, not a package), question setuptools (usually not a runtime dep)
quiz.explain: Unpinned deps make builds non-reproducible; asyncio is stdlib; setuptools is a build tool. The MR needs == pins across the board.

quiz.q: In a Dockerfile, you replace a cleanup RUN (rm -rf /tmp/build) with RUN echo hello. Does the image get smaller?
choices: No — each RUN is a layer; files removed in a later layer are whiteout-hidden but still present in earlier layers, and echo adds its own layer
quiz.explain: Layers are additive; deletion in a later layer whiteouts but does not reclaim earlier-layer bytes. Cleanup must happen in the SAME RUN that created the files.

quiz.q: Why does the panel ask 'how many services can run in a pod'?
choices: To check you know one pod = one logical host: one main container plus sidecars (logging, proxy) sharing network/storage — not many independent apps
quiz.explain: The pod is the atomic unit: tightly-coupled containers sharing localhost and volumes. Independent apps get separate pods/deployments.

quiz.q: Single-threaded Python service fails readiness probes under load; the Java equivalent does not. Likely cause?
choices: The GIL: the single thread blocks on CPU work so the probe handler cannot respond in time — separate probe handling/async or more replicas
quiz.explain: GIL-bound single-threaded servers serialize request handling and probe responses; under load the probe times out. Async frameworks, thread pools for probes, or horizontal scaling fix it.

quiz.q: Closing a panel: which is strongest?
choices: Ask two genuine questions (on-call load, their Terraform workflow), then close: 'This is exactly the boundary work I do best'
quiz.explain: Genuine operational questions signal senior thinking; the close restates fit in one line. Compensation comes through the recruiter, not the panel.

drills.title: Timed drill: technical rapid-fire (90s each, aloud)

items.prompt: Terraform vs Ansible: biggest difference; if Ansible can create VMs why not just use Ansible; difference removing resources; what exactly do you do in the TF file to remove a resource?
items.answer: Terraform is declarative desired-state with state tracking; Ansible is procedural task execution. Ansible can create VMs but has no state — it cannot plan/detect drift the way Terraform does. Removing: in Ansible you write the absent-state task; in Terraform you delete the block (or use a removed block) and apply. In the TF file: delete the resource block and run terraform apply to destroy it — or add a removed { from = ... lifecycle { destroy = false } } block to drop it from state without destroying.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Terraform manages desired state with a state file — plan shows the diff, apply converges, drift is detectable. Ansible executes ordered tasks idempotently but keeps no state, so it cannot plan or show you what changed. That is why Ansible provisions but Terraform owns lifecycle. To remove: delete the resource block and apply — Terraform destroys it. If you must keep the real resource (the data-disk drift case), use a removed block with destroy=false so Terraform forgets it without deleting it.'

items.prompt: Preferred OS? Red Hat familiarity / Satellite? df shows free space but 'no space left on device' — causes? Other intermittent causes with free space?
items.answer: RHEL (familiar; Satellite for patch/content management at fleet scale). df-free-but-full: inodes exhausted (df -i); deleted-but-open files (lsof +L1); quotas; /tmp on a separate full mount.
items.explain: Model answer: 'RHEL — I am comfortable with it, and Satellite for centralized patching and provisioning across fleets. "No space" with free blocks: first df -i — inode exhaustion from millions of small files. Second lsof +L1 — deleted files held open by processes still consume space. Third quotas, fourth a full /tmp mount. Intermittent with free space: a log rotation racing disk usage, or a process holding deleted files that releases on restart — which is why the failure comes and goes.'

items.prompt: Check open ports? Simplest tool to check a port from server A to server B? Troubleshoot connection issues between two servers? UDP vs TCP?
items.answer: ss -tlnp / netstat -tlnp / lsof -i -P. A→B: telnet host port or nc -vz host port. Triage: ping (L3), traceroute (path), telnet/nc (port), firewall rules both ends. UDP: connectionless, no handshake/ordering; TCP: handshake, ordered, reliable.
items.explain: Model answer: 'ss -tlnp is my default — sockets, listening TCP, numeric, with process. Server A to B: telnet or nc -vz — the connection result IS the test. Between servers: ping for reachability, traceroute for the path, telnet to the port for the service, then firewall rules and security groups on both ends. UDP vs TCP: UDP is fire-and-forget datagrams — no handshake, no ordering, no retransmission — good for DNS and voice; TCP handshakes and guarantees ordered delivery — good for everything requiring correctness.'

items.prompt: Rebase vs merge?
items.answer: Merge preserves full history with a merge commit; rebase rewrites commits onto the target for linear history. Rebase private branches, merge shared ones.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Merge keeps the true history including the merge commit — safe for shared branches. Rebase replays my commits on top of the target for a clean linear log — but it rewrites SHAs, so only on branches nobody else uses. Rule: rebase to clean up my own work, merge to integrate shared work.'

items.prompt:
Read this script, predict the output, and state how many Kia cars print:
cars = ['Kia Soul','Toyota Camry','Kia Forte','Honda Civic','Kia Sorento']
kia_count = 0
for car in cars:
    brand = car.split()[0]
    if brand == 'Kia':
        kia_count += 1
        print(f'Kia found: {car}')
    else:
