print(f'Total Kias: {kia_count}')
Second: review requirements.txt (requests, flask, flask-cors, asyncio, setuptools, pandas, pytest — all unpinned). Approve the MR? What must change?
items.answer: Output: Kia found: Kia Soul / Other: Toyota / Kia found: Kia Forte / Other: Honda / Kia found: Kia Sorento / Total Kias: 3. Three Kias. MR: request changes — pin all versions (==), remove asyncio (stdlib), question setuptools as a runtime dep.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Trace: split()[0] takes the brand; Kia matches three times — Soul, Forte, Sorento — each prints and increments; others print the brand; final line prints 3. On the MR: I would not approve — unpinned dependencies make builds non-reproducible, asyncio is standard library and does not belong in requirements, and setuptools is a build tool, not a runtime dependency. Require == pins on everything and drop asyncio.'

items.prompt: Optimize container image size? What does RUN do in a Dockerfile? Replace a cleanup RUN with RUN echo hello — does the size change? Does removing files in a later layer reduce size?
items.answer: Multi-stage builds, minimal base (slim/distroless), combine RUNs, .dockerignore. RUN creates a layer. No — echo adds a layer and cleanup must be in the same RUN. No — whiteout hides but earlier layers retain bytes.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Optimize with multi-stage builds, minimal bases, combined RUN statements, and .dockerignore. Each RUN creates an immutable layer. Replacing cleanup with echo hello does not shrink anything — it adds a layer. And removing files in a later layer only whiteouts them: the bytes remain in the earlier layer, so the image stays large. Cleanup belongs in the SAME RUN that created the files.'

items.prompt: Troubleshoot an app in a pod? Pod keeps restarting — next steps? Check exit code and reason? Container svc-basic terminated exit code 137 — why?
items.answer: kubectl get/describe/logs/exec + events. Restart loop: describe lastState reason/exit code, logs --previous, probes, resources. Exit code + reason: describe pod → lastState.terminated. 137 = OOMKilled (128+9 SIGKILL): over memory limit.
items.explain: Model answer: 'kubectl describe for events and lastState, logs --previous for the crash output, exec only if it stays up. Restarting: read lastState.terminated reason and exit code first — that names it. 137 is 128+9, SIGKILL — in Kubernetes that is the OOM killer enforcing the memory limit. Fix: raise the limit or fix the leak, and check the request/limit math from the YAML review.'

items.prompt: Pod YAML review: image nginx:v4, requests memory 16Gi cpu 0.5, limits memory 32Gi cpu 8. Issues? If nginx needs min 2Gi to start, does it work? Request 1Gi but needs 2Gi — works? How many services/apps per pod?
items.answer: 16Gi request is enormous for nginx — wasteful, blocks scheduling; :v4 is an unpinned mutable tag; cpu 0.5 request vs 8 limit is a huge burst ratio. 2Gi need with 16Gi request: schedules and runs (over-provisioned). 1Gi request, 2Gi need: schedules, then OOMKilled. One logical app per pod + sidecars.
items.explain: Model answer: 'The 16Gi request for nginx is wildly over-provisioned — it reserves memory the app will never use and can block scheduling; the :v4 tag is unpinned; the request/limit spread invites noisy-neighbor issues. With a 2Gi minimum need and 16Gi requested: yes, it runs — over-provisioned but fine. With 1Gi requested and 2Gi needed: it schedules (requests are met) then OOMKills at runtime — requests gate scheduling, limits gate survival. And a pod holds one logical application plus its sidecars — independent apps get their own pods.'

drills.title: Timed drill: deep technical + STAR behavioral (2 min each, aloud)

items.prompt: Jenkins pipelines: with what tools/languages? Groovy directly in the Jenkinsfile? Standardize Jenkinsfiles across repos? Have you written shared libraries?
items.answer: Declarative pipelines, Groovy (scripted or shared-library code); yes Groovy directly; standardize via shared libraries (vars/ + src/); describe one you wrote: e.g. a standardBuild() step with checkout/test/scan/push.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Declarative pipelines, with Groovy for scripted logic. Yes — Groovy goes directly in the Jenkinsfile for simple cases, but to standardize across repos I wrote a shared library: a vars/standardBuild.groovy wrapping checkout, unit tests, Semgrep, Trivy scan, and image push, with src/ helpers for the retry logic. Repos then declare a five-line Jenkinsfile calling standardBuild with parameters — one place to update the gate policy for all services.'

items.prompt: Why Helm instead of plain YAML?
items.answer: Templating + values per environment, versioned releases with rollback, chart dependencies, lifecycle hooks — plain YAML duplicates per environment and has no release concept.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Plain YAML means a copy per environment that drifts. Helm gives parameterized templates with values files per env, versioned releases I can rollback with one command, and chart dependencies for shared components. For a handful of static manifests plain YAML is fine; past that, Helm is the release engineering answer.'

items.prompt: Self-rate your Terraform. Walk the full lifecycle testing→dev→stage→QA→prod. Scenario: dev team needs a storage account with given container names — codify it. Requirements change to per-container access types — modify the code. State drift: a VM data disk was added manually in Azure and must be kept — what do you do? Show the for_each import address escaping.
items.answer: Rating with justification + feature branches/PR plan/apply per env with gates. Storage: resource + for_each over list; change: for_each over map(name→access). Drift: plan, import to keep, then codify. Import: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]' <id>.
items.explain: Model answer (STAR-shaped): 'I would rate myself [honest level] — I have owned Terraform end to end: modules in GitHub, PR-driven plans, per-environment workspaces, applies gated through Jenkins with credentials injected, secrets via env vars and Vault, tfvars never committed, Consul for service discovery config. Lifecycle: feature branch → plan on PR → apply to dev on merge → promote the same artifact through stage and QA with environment tfvars → prod apply behind approval. Storage scenario: azurerm_storage_account plus azurerm_storage_container with for_each over the name list; when access types diverge, refactor to for_each over a map of name→access type. Drift: terraform plan surfaces it; to keep the manual disk I run terraform import with the for_each address quoted — terraform import \'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]\' <id> — then codify the resource so the next plan is clean. The quoting matters: the shell must not eat the brackets.'

items.prompt: How were K8s endpoints exposed via Application Gateway? Expose an internal Azure endpoint to the internet? App Gateway vs Load Balancer? Walk the traffic flow browser→DNS→App Gateway→backend. Private Links: for which services? Private link custom DNS?
items.answer: AGIC programs AppGW from Ingress. Internal→internet: public AppGW/WAF or LB with public IP + NSG. L7 vs L4. Flow: DNS→AppGW public IP→TLS+host/path routing→backend pool→pod. Private Link: storage, SQL, Key Vault, App Service, ACR. DNS: Private DNS zone + A record + VNet link (+ conditional forwarding).
items.explain: Model answer: 'AGIC watches Ingress and programs the Application Gateway — host/path routing at Layer 7 with TLS termination and WAF. To expose an internal endpoint: a public Application Gateway (or public LB) with locked-down NSGs in front of it. App Gateway is L7 HTTP; Load Balancer is L4 TCP/UDP. Traffic: browser resolves DNS to the gateway IP, the gateway terminates TLS, matches host/path, and forwards to the AKS backend pool, where kube-proxy reaches the pod. Private Link exposes PaaS privately — storage, SQL, Key Vault, App Service, ACR — via a private endpoint; custom DNS needs a Private DNS zone with the A record, linked to the VNet, so the PaaS FQDN resolves to the private IP.'

items.prompt: Ansible: manage others' playbooks or write new? Most interesting role you created? How do you capture command output?
items.answer: Both — inherit carefully, write idempotently. Interesting role: describe concretely (e.g. hardened CIS baseline role with handlers). Capture: register the task result, then use stdout/debug or a follow-up task.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Both — I have inherited playbooks, which means reading for idempotence gaps and variable contracts before changing anything, and I have written roles from scratch. The most interesting was a CIS-hardening role: parameterized by profile level, with handlers restarting only affected services and molecule tests proving idempotence. Output capture: register the result — register: cmd_out — then reference cmd_out.stdout in debug or a conditional follow-up task.'

items.prompt: Benefit of multiple node pools vs one giant pool? Pod stuck in Pending — troubleshoot? 'Insufficient resources' / 'out of nodes' — fix? Manually increase max nodes per pool? New nodes still not deploying — your checklist? Taint vs toleration vs label? Pod Running then suddenly restarts — which probe? Single-threaded Python vs Java readiness failures — why? Service knocked over under load failing health checks — cloud-native recommendations?
items.answer: Pools: SKU/scaling/blast-radius/cost separation. Pending: describe events. Out of nodes: raise max-count. Manual: az aks nodepool update --max-count. Checklist: autoscaler logs, quotas, region capacity, taints, labels, identity perms, Activity log, Monitor/Health, subnet IPs, SKU restrictions, Policy, max pods. Taint repels/toleration permits/label attracts. Liveness restarts. GIL blocks probe handler. Recommendations: async/non-blocking, separate probe endpoints, timeouts.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Multiple pools: separate VM SKUs, independent autoscaler bounds, smaller upgrade blast radius, spot mixing, workload isolation. Pending: kubectl describe, read FailedScheduling. Out of nodes with pool at max: az aks nodepool update --max-count higher. Still no nodes: autoscaler logs, vCPU quota, region capacity, taints/tolerations, label selectors, identity permissions, Activity log failures, Azure Monitor/Resource Health, subnet IP exhaustion, SKU restrictions, Azure Policy, max pods per node. Taints repel, tolerations permit, labels attract. Running-then-restarting is the liveness probe. Python readiness failures under load: the GIL — the single thread cannot serve the probe while busy. Knocked-over service: async non-blocking handlers, dedicated lightweight probe endpoints, timeouts everywhere, and horizontal scaling — so health checks answer even when the app is saturated.'

items.prompt: Major pipeline phases commit→release? Where is the most code stopped? Strangler fig a monolithic trading platform? Fault tolerance for mission-critical financial apps? Logging/monitoring at millions of txns/sec? RBAC across the full stack?
items.answer: Phases: commit→build→unit test→SAST/SCA→artifact→deploy staging→DAST/E2E→prod w/ gates. Most stopped: unit tests. Strangler: seam by seam, gateway-routed, dual-write data. HA: multi-AZ + tested multi-region, data replication binding. Scale: sampling+aggregation. RBAC: least privilege per layer.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Commit triggers build and unit tests — where most code is stopped, cheapest. Then SAST/SCA gates, artifact build, staging deploy, DAST and end-to-end, production behind approval with burn-rate auto-rollback. Strangler fig: extract seam by seam starting with read-only services, gateway-routed percentages with monolith fallback, data via dual-write, retire at zero traffic — never a big bang. Mission-critical HA: multi-AZ everywhere, active-passive multi-region with rehearsed failover, data replication as the binding constraint. Millions of txns/sec: sampling and aggregation architecture — bounded cardinality, recording rules, sampled logs, tail-sampled traces. RBAC: least privilege at every layer — K8s roles, cloud IAM, app roles, database grants, pipeline approvals.'

items.prompt: STAR: a time you translated unclear business requirements into technical deliverables. STAR: a time you introduced a new technology improving team performance. STAR: a time you mentored developers. And: do you prefer coding or infrastructure?
items.answer: Three STAR stories (spec→validate→ship; PoC→demo→pair→adopt; curriculum→solo on-call) + honest boundary answer: code in service of reliability.
items.explain: Model answers: (1) Requirements — Situation: ops asked for 'better deployment visibility.' Task: make it shippable. Action: interviewed three on-call engineers, mapped pain to golden signals, wrote a one-page spec, validated before building, shipped in two sprints. Result: deploy correlation down to 5 minutes; the spec format became the team template. (2) New tech — Situation: hand-edited YAML per environment. Task: safer pattern. Action: Kustomize PoC on one service, team demo, migration guide, paired each owner through conversion. Result: misconfigurations fell; new-service onboarding from a day to an hour; all 12 services migrated. (3) Mentoring — Situation: juniors struggling with on-call. Task: get them confident. Action: weekly 30-min curriculum — dashboards, runbook hands-on, simulated incident they commanded. Result: two juniors on solo on-call in two months, zero first-rotation escalations. Coding vs infrastructure: 'I am happiest at the boundary — I write code that operates infrastructure: automation, exporters, pipeline logic. My best days are when code I wrote at 10 AM prevents a 2 AM page.'

handsOnLab.title: Lab: run the full 90-minute mock panel solo
handsOnLab.brief: You will execute the complete mock panel script from the notes — timed, aloud, recorded, with no aids — then score every answer against the rubric, red-team the weak ones, and re-drill until the bank is green.
steps: Print the 90-minute script (notes 5-6) and the scoring rubric; set up a timer and a recorder (phone is fine).
Round 1 (10 min): deliver the 60-second intro and the 2-minute proudest-project STAR — recorded, no notes.
Round 2 (20 min): answer all 8 Terraform/IaC questions aloud at 90 seconds each; mark red/yellow/green immediately after each.
Round 3 (15 min): Linux/networking/Docker rapid-fire — same timing and scoring.
Round 4 (20 min): Kubernetes/AKS round including the YAML math and the node-provisioning checklist.
Round 5 (15 min): CI/CD, Jenkins, Helm, security gates, secrets, RBAC.
Round 6 (10 min): architecture and scale — strangler fig, HA, millions-of-txns observability, multicloud strategy.
Round 7 (15 min): the four behavioral questions at 2 minutes each, STAR-structured, recorded.
Round 8 (5 min): ask your two panel questions aloud and deliver the one-line close.
Score every answer 1-5 on accuracy, completeness, structure, delivery; total out of 160; passing bar 120 with no reds on safety-critical items.
For every red/yellow: handwrite the full model answer from the drills, then re-drill it cold the next day.
Within 24 hours, write the debrief: three strongest answers, three weakest, and the exact study plan for the week.
Repeat weekly; the question bank stays in rotation until every item is green three sessions running.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A recorded 90-minute mock panel, a completed 160-point rubric, handwritten red-team corrections, and a weekly study plan.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Total score ≥120 with zero reds on safety-critical items (secrets, RBAC, blast radius); every red from the prior session re-drilled to green.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'Do you prefer coding or infrastructure?' Which response is strongest?
choices: 'I hate coding — just give me the consoles'
'I only want to write application features'

'I am strongest at the boundary: I write code that operates infrastructure — automation, tooling, pipeline logic. My best work is code that prevents 2 AM pages, which is exactly this team's platform work.'
mockTask.explain: STAR-shaped reasoning: the Situation is a DevSecOps platform role; the Task is showing fit; the Action is the honest, specific preference (code in service of reliability) with evidence (automation, exporters, runbooks); the Result is the bridge — 'which is exactly this team's platform work.' It is specific, honest, and role-tied. The other options are disqualifying (anti-coding), misaligned (pure app dev), or empty (hedged non-answer).
